attributes.description: See Black Cultural Center, GIS ID #334

attributes.Name: 501 Hayes Street
attributes.description: Now Delta Chi

attributes.Name: Sreum Laboratory
attributes.description:
THIS BUILDING DID NOT EXIST! SERUM LABORATORY GONE AFTER 1941!
This structure actually consists of two (connected) buildings from 1949 - 1980: Veterinary Postmortem Laboratory and Animal Disease Diagnostics Laboratory.

attributes.Name: Wayne T. and Mary T. Hockmeyer Hall of Structural Biology
attributes.description: Hockmeyer Hall includes eight specialized labs and eight general labs for work in the areas of protein production, cell and virus culture, large molecule crystallization, X-ray diffraction, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, electron microscopy, and analytical and biophysical instrumentation.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Hockmeyer Hall is named for Wayne T. Hockmeyer and his wife, Mary, who gave $5.3 million toward its construction.

attributes.Name: Football Practice Trainer's Building
attributes.description: This Football Practice Trainer's Building was located south of the football training fields. It was demolished in 2016 to make room for the new Football Performance Center. The new performance center is an expansion of the Mollenkopf Athletic Center.

attributes.Name: Schowe House
attributes.description: The original Schowe House was built in 1929 by J.C. Allen. Then, in 1990, the house was purchased by Purdue Professor Kent Fuchs and his wife, Linda. The couple added a west wing to the house and made other improvements. Later, in June 2003, alumni Tom and Anne Schowe purchased the home to live closer to Purdue while their daughter Christina was attending the university. Finally, in 2009, the house became the new center for Purdue's Global Policy Research Institute. The cost and square footage of the home is unknown.
attributes.dedicationinfo: In 2009 the home was dedicated and named after the Schowe family.

attributes.Name: Schowe House Garage
attributes.description: The Schowe House garage is part of the Schowe House on Northwestern Avenue that was built by J. C. Allen in 1929. In 1990 the house and garage were purchased by Purdue Professor Kent Fuchs and his wife, Linda. In 2009 the house became the new center for Purdue's Global Policy Research Institute.

attributes.Name: Bill and Sally Hanley Hall
attributes.description: Bill and Sally Hanley Hall was built in 2011 and is dedicated to studying families, children, and human development. The building contains the Military Family Research Institute, the Purdue Center on Aging and the Life Course, and the Ben and Maxine Miller Child Development Laboratory School, and the department of Human Development and Family Studies.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building was dedicated to Bill and Sally Hanley who donated $3 million to the buildings construction. Sally Berner Hanley graduated from Purdue with a degree in home economics and child development in 1961.

attributes.Name: Guy J. Mackey Arena
attributes.description: A major addition was added to the Guy J. Mackey Arena in 2011. During this renovation, the arena and adjoining facilities were renovated. The arena also remained open and home to male and female sports during the construction process.
attributes.dedicationinfo: On Nov. 10, 2011, Mackey Arena was formally rededicated, with subsequent re-dedication games for the men's and women's basketball teams on November 11 and 13.

attributes.Name: Hangar No. 6
attributes.description: An addition was added to Hangar No. 6 in 1991. This addition was added to accommodate the growing flight training program.  The expansion included additions to the north and west end of the existing hangar that would be used for aircraft maintenance. During the addition, a sprinkler system was also added to the hangar.

attributes.Name: Northwest Chiller Plant
attributes.description: The Northwest Chiller Plant was constructed from 2001 to 2003.

attributes.Name: Turf Recreation Exercise Center
attributes.description: The Turf Recreation Exercise Center was built in 2011. It includes a locker room, mechanical room, and an artificial turf surface.

attributes.Name: ADM Agricultural Innovation Center
attributes.description: The ADM Agricultural Innovation Center was built in 2011 to allow students to gain more experience with large agricultural machinery. The building contains classrooms, a conference room, machine and fabrication services, and space for the Department of Agricultural and Biological Engineering and the Central Machine Shop.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building is dedicated to the Archer Daniels Midland (ADM) Company who donated $1.5 million to the building in 2011. ADM is a longstanding partner with Purdue in the education of agricultural and biological engineering and agricultural systems management students.

attributes.Name: Transportation Service Wash Facility
attributes.description: The Transportation Service Wash Facility is located southeast of the Physical Facilities Service Building. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Herrick Laboratories
attributes.description: The Herrick Laboratories is located east of the original Herrick building on Russell Drive. This building was built to double to size of mechanical engineering laboratory space. The building also houses the Federal Aviation Administration, the Center for High Performance Buildings, and a large living laboratory. The building is also a LEED-GOLD certified building and is used to research human-building interactions.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building is named after Raymond W. Herrick who researched, housed conferences in, and funded students interested in the fields of heating, ventilation, air-conditioning, and refrigeration. A laboratory inside the building is also named after Willis Carrier who founded the Carrier ventilation company and invented modern air conditioning.

attributes.Name: Bailey Hall
attributes.description: Bailey Hall is the home for the Purdue Musical Organizations  (PMO) and was built in 2014. The building contains rehearsal rooms, lounges, study areas, a music library, and an environmentally controlled storage space. Before moving to Bailey Hall, the PMO were housed in the Elliot Hall of Music.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building was dedicated to Ralph and Bettye Bailey. The Baileys made a generous donation towards the construction of the facility. Ralph Bailey graduated with a degree in Mechanical Engineering from Purdue University. The dedication included speeches from Ralph Bailey, Purdue President Mitch Daniels, Purdue Musical Organizations (PMO) director William Griffel, and several others. There were also performances done by the PMO six choral ensembles. A student lounge in the building is also named in memory of the PMO founder Dr. Albert P. Stewart.

attributes.Name: Seng-Liang Weng Hall
attributes.description: Seng-Liang Weng Hall houses research laboratories for the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering. It is also leased by the Purdue Research Foundation (PRF) to private businesses and the University. It also forms the "ECE triangle" along with the Electrical Engineering Building and the Materials and Electrical Engineering Building.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building is dedicated to Patrick Wang who received a bachelors and masters degree from Purdue in electrical engineering. Wang is now the CEO and chairmen of the Johnson Electric Group.

attributes.Name: Harrison Street Parking Garage
attributes.description: The Harrison Street Parking Garage was constructed to accommodate 850 vehicles. It was constructed along with Human and Health Sciences Research Facility (Lyles-Porter Hall).

attributes.Name: Lyles-Porter Hall
attributes.description: Originally called the Health and Human Sciences Research Facility, Lyles-Porter Hall was built in 2012. The building houses multiple departments including the Department of Speech, Language and Hearing Sciences, School of Nursing, Nutrition Science, Psychological Science, and Health and Kinesiology. The building contains classrooms, offices, the M.D. Steer Audiology and Speech-Language Clinics, the Indiana University Medical School, the A.H. Ismail Center for Health, Exercise and Nutrition, a Nursing Center for Family Health, and a Nutritional Training and Research Center.  Outside of the building is also an outdoor learning space that encourages communication between children.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Lyles-Porter Hall was dedicated to George A. Porter and William M. Lyles who earned degrees in civil engineering in 1922 and 1935 respectively. Both Porter and Lyle were family members of Marybeth Lyles-Porter Seay who made a generous donation to the University in their honor. Seay herself, and many of her other family members, were also Purdue Alumni.

attributes.Name: Bindley Bioscience Center
attributes.description: An addition to the Bindley Bioscience Center was completed in 2013. It was a 29,000-square-foot, two-story expansion and added the Multidisciplinary Cancer Research Facility. It allowed Purdue to work on innovative animal models of disease, development of new therapeutics, and work with in-vivo animal imaging.

attributes.Name: Krach Leadership Center
attributes.description: The Krach Leadership Center is a LEED-Gold Certified building that was completed in 2014. The Center contains spaces for student organizations, conference rooms, study areas, and special events. The building was built to encourage leadership and academic success on campus.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building is named after Keith Krach who was a Chairman on the Board of Trustees at Purdue University from 2007-2013. Krach graduated from Purdue with a degree in industrial engineering in 1979 and was the chairmen and/or CEO of many companies including DocuSign, Angie's List, and Ariba. Krach and his wife, Metta, gave many generous donations to the university and Krach was known for his philanthropic service and leadership.

attributes.Name: Purdue Hall
attributes.description: Purdue Hall, originally called the Dormitory or Men's Dormitory, was utilized for many purposes and included dormitory rooms, classrooms, and museums. It was a four-story building with 32 rooms and accommodated 80 students. It was also modeled after the Massachusetts Agricultural College Dormitory. In 1902, the north end was remodeled in order to add more classroom space to the university. It was at this point that the building began to be referred to as Purdue Hall. The building was demolished in 1961 at a cost of $4,746.

attributes.Name: Engineering Administration Building
attributes.description: The third floor was added to the Service and Stores Building in 1938.

attributes.Name: Oliver Perkins Terry House (OB1)
attributes.description: An addition was added to the west end of the Oliver Perkins Terry House in 1977. It added a loading dock and small overhang. In 1994 the building was vacated and renovated for the use of the Purdue University police department.

attributes.Name: Administrative Services Building
attributes.description: The Administrative Services Building was built on South Grant Street, immediately north of the Wade Utility Plant. When it was built, it was approximately 100,000 sq. ft., had no interior walls and no private offices in any of the office areas.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Administrative Services building was renamed the Lytle J. Freehafer Hall of Administrative in honor of Mr. Freehafer in recognition of his work in university administrative services and impact upon the University.

attributes.Name: Purdue Technology Center Aerospace
attributes.description: The Purdue Technology Center Aerospace (PTCA) building was built in 2017. It was built as part of the Purdue Research Park Aerospace District and contains Rolls-Royce research on jet engines.

attributes.Name: Honors College and Residences North
attributes.description: The Honors College and Residences North is a residence hall that was built in 2016. The Honors College and Residences are comprised of single, double, and triple rooms, shared bathrooms, and lounges. The residence hall also focuses on developing learning communities where students can live with a community of students who are committed to academic success.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The $90 million Purdue Honors College was dedicated on September 12, 2016.

attributes.Name: Honors College and Residences South
attributes.description: The Honors College and Residences South is a residence hall that was built in 2016. The Honors College and Residences are comprised of single, double, and triple rooms, shared bathrooms, and lounges. The residence hall also focuses on developing learning communities where students can live with a community of students who are committed to academic success.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The $90 million Purdue Honors College was dedicated on September 12, 2016.

attributes.Name: Hobart and Russell Creighton Hall of Animal Sciences
attributes.description: The Hobart and Russell Creighton Hall of Animal Sciences was built in 2017. The building is a three-story structure focused on improving food and animal safety and efficiency. The building contains laboratories, classrooms, conference rooms, and offices. The building also houses the Department of Animal Science, the U.S. Department of Agriculture-Agricultural Research Service's Livestock Behavior Unit, and staff of Indiana animal regulatory agencies.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Groundbreaking ceremony was on November 6, 2015. The building was dedicated in honor of Hobart and Russell Creighton who were brothers and founders of the Creighton Brothers company. The Creighton Family gifted money to the university for the creation of the building in honor of the founders of the egg production company.

attributes.Name: Flex Lab Facility
attributes.description: The Flex Lab is a 75,000 square foot collaborative research facility for the College of Engineering that focuses on research in fields such as manufacturing, imaging, information technology, and medical devices. The building was created to encourage collaboration between the College of Engineering and industry- and government-funded research. The Flex Lab houses wet-labs, dry-labs, and open collaboration spaces. It was supported by a $13.5 million donation from Eli Lilly and Company.

attributes.Name: Controlled Environment Phenotyping Facility
attributes.description: The Controlled Environment Phenotyping Facility is a new research building for the college of Agriculture. The building was created to be a plant imaging facility with controlled growing environments. It was part of the Purdue Moves initiative to expand plant sciences. The building contains two growth chambers with automated imaging stations, conveyors and robots that allow plants to be imaged, moved, and cared for.

attributes.Name: Bechtel Innovation Design Center
attributes.description: The Bechtel Innovation Design Center is a hands-on learning center for students in the College of Engineering and the Purdue Polytechnic Institute. It encourages collaboration and allows students to design, build, and test various projects in the indoor spaces and outdoor plaza. The center contains open work spaces, labs, offices, studios, and storage spaces. The space also contains various tools that students can use to complete their various designs.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building is dedicated to Stephen D. Bechtel, Jr. who gave a generous donation towards the construction of the building.  Bechtel was also a Purdue graduate who received a bachelor's degree in civil engineering in 1946 and honorary doctorate in 1972.

attributes.Name: Chaffee Hall
attributes.description: Chaffee Hall is a two-story, T-shaped library and office building completed in 1967. The building is located at the Jet Propulsion Center west of the Purdue airport, which is now Zucrow Labs. The building contains a lecture room, offices, a library, a storage vault, laboratories, and a drafting room.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Chaffee Hall was named after Roger B. Chaffee, a Navy pilot and NASA astronaut, who lost his life in a NASA pre-launch fire at Cape Kennedy in 1967.

attributes.Name: Grand Prix Track
attributes.description: In 1969 a permanent Grand Prix racetrack was created. Previously, the race track was in the Ross-Ade Stadium parking lot but it needed to be moved during the expansion of the stadium. This new, smaller, safer, and more interesting race track was constructed at the corner of Cherry Lane and Northwestern Avenue. This new race track also included temporary bleachers and a permanent fence.

attributes.Name: John and Anna Margaret Ross Alexander Field
attributes.description: The Purdue Baseball stadium was completed in 2012 and held it's first game on March 22, 2013 against Ohio State. It is located within the Northwest Athletic Complex on Cherry Lane and between US 231 and McCormick Road. The stadium replaced Lambert Field and can hold 1,500-2,500 spectators. The baseball stadium also contains a locker room, team meeting room, indoor hitting facility, and the Charles & Susan Armstrong Sports Medicine room. The dugout is named in honor of the Omholt family.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The baseball field is named after John and Anna Margaret Ross Alexander. Dave Alexander, the son of John and Anna Margaret, was a Purdue baseball coach and athletics administrator. He also made a generous donation to the university for the baseball stadium.

attributes.Name: Bittinger Stadium
attributes.description: The Bittinger Stadium is located within the Northwest Athletic Complex and is adjacent to Alexander Field. The first game was held on March 20, 2015 against Wisconsin. It contains the playing field, bleachers, press box, locker rooms, meeting rooms, heated dugouts, and an athletic training treatment area. It was built to hold 1,000 fans but can be expanded for NCAA post-season competitions.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The stadium was named in honor of Professor Marvin L. and Elaine Bittinger on December 19, 2016. Professor Bittinger graduated from Purdue in 1968 with a degree in mathematics. He was also an author, professor, and strong supporter of Purdue.

attributes.Name: Dennis J. and Mary Lou Schwartz Tennis Center
attributes.description: The Dennis J. and Mary Lou Schwartz Tennis Center was officially opened on December 30, 2006. It contains six indoor courts, twelve outdoor courts, locker rooms, offices, an athletic training center, and seating areas. The courts are made of a special Plexiplave material which gives extra support to players' legs during matches.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The tennis courts are dedicated to Dennis J. and Mary Lou Schwartz. Dennis Schwartz obtained a bachelors' in industrial engineering in 1963 and worked as a banking executive. Mr. Schwarz made a large donation towards the building in honor of his wife, Mary Lou Schwartz, who was a devoted tennis player.

attributes.Name: Folk Field
attributes.description: Folk Field, originally the Varsity Soccer Complex, was built in 1998. At this time, two fields were constructed, one for games and one for practices, in order to reduce the amount of wear to the field. Folk Field was remodeled in 2007 to improve the drainage system and add Bermuda grass. During this renovation, Plexiglass shelters were also added. In 2011, lights were installed to allow for night games. In 2012, the complex was heavily remodeled and a new building was added. The new structure contains locker rooms, meeting rooms, an athletic training room, and press box. The locker room has many amenities such as a flat-screen TV, mini fridge, and personalized lockers. The complex also contains a press box, meeting rooms, concessions stands, bathrooms, and grand stands.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Folk Field was named after Loren and Donna Folk. The Folks were both generous supporters of Purdue.

attributes.Name: Combustion Research Laboratory
attributes.description: The Combustion Research Laboratory was built in 1953 and contains office space for Dr. Zucrow, his assistants, two secretaries, and several graduate students. An instructional classroom was also created to house the growing number of graduate students in the program. This building is also part of the Maurice J. Zucrow Laboratories Complex that was named after it's founder.

attributes.Name: Gas Dynamics Research Laboratory
attributes.description: The Gas Dynamics Research Laboratory provided space for an enlarged machine shop, three gas turbine component test cells and control rooms, two Navy surplus high-pressure air compressors, a welding shop, and an experimental equipment assembly room. A new addition was later added to replace the two high-pressure air compressors. This building is part of the Maurice J. Zucrow Laboratories Complex that was named after it's founder.

attributes.Name: High Pressure Research Laboratory
attributes.description: The High Pressure Research Laboratory was built to accommodate experimental rocket motors. The building contained a test cell building connected to a control room by a long passage. It also housed experimental system controls, two rocket motor test cells, high pressure propellant tanks, and propellant piping. This building is part of the Maurice J. Zucrow Laboratories Complex that was named after it's founder.

attributes.Name: Turbomachinery Fluid Dynamics Laboratory
attributes.description: The Turbomachinery Fluid Dynamics Laboratory is part of the Maurice J. Zucrow Laboratories complex.

attributes.Name: Grand Prix Track
attributes.description: The Grand Prix track was moved to its present location at the corner of McCormick Road and Cherry Lane in 2009 to make room for the addition to Mackey Arena. The new stadium contains the track, stands for spectators, and a restroom facility. The first race held on the new track was in 2009 for the fifty-second annual Grand Prix. The new track is four feet wider than the original track to make additional space for all of the kart crews and the race crew.

attributes.Name: Purdue Crew Boathouse
attributes.description: The Levee Boathouse is a new facility for the Purdue Crew Team located on the Wabash River near Tapawingo Park. The new, two-story boat house was built to replace the old boathouse that was built in 1949. The building contains a foyer, five bays (four for boats and one for maintenance), two workout areas, and multiple bathrooms. One bay is also used to allow the public to rent storage space for their canoes and kayaks.

attributes.Name: Purdue Memorial Union
attributes.description: A major addition was added to the Purdue Memorial Union in 1940. During this expansion, the west wing was constructed which doubled the size of ballroom space (added the North ballroom) and created additional dining rooms and student organization offices. Construction of the east wing doubled the Union Club living facilities to 126 rooms and the bowling alley was also renovated.

attributes.Name: Recreational Gymnasium
attributes.description: An addition was added to the Recreational Gymnasium in 1983. It added 8 racquetball courts and 3 basketball courts.

attributes.Name: Printing Services
attributes.description: The Printing Services building was built near the Single and Marriage Student Housing Courts and served as a storage facility. Over its existence, the structure has several purposes. It was originally called the Family Housing and Central Machine shop and was renamed the Family Housing and Property Accounting Warehouse in 1969. The structure became the home of Central Duplicating (later known as Printing Services) in 1972. Following the creation of a new Printing Services facility, this building was demolished as the university began plans to construct Hockmeyer Hall of Structural Biology.

attributes.Name: Service Annex and Central Machine Shop
attributes.description: The Service Annex and Central Machine Shop was built on the south end of campus. It was funded by the Federal Works Administration along with many other buildings. It was acquired from the Vigo Ordnance Plant and was a transite storage building. This building was reduced in size in 1997 as part of a plan to relocate the Facilities Service operation to south of the main campus. This made room for more academic buildings on the southern edge of campus. The building was torn down completely in 2012 to make room for Lyles-Porter Hall.

attributes.Name: Golf Starter House
attributes.description: The first golf starter house was built in 1951. It was torn down in 1986 to make room for a women's locker room.

attributes.Name: Heating and Power Plant North
attributes.description: The North Power Plant was added onto for the first time in 1932. The addition made space for boilers to be added to the plant. On April 19, 1932 there was a fire in the addition of the building. The "damage was not serious, most of it consisted of (a) burned pipe covering; (and) that two grinders had warped and would probably have to be replaced." The loss was fully covered by insurance and the cost of damage was about $7000. On February 12, 1938 the chimney was damaged due to a lightning strike.

attributes.Name: Robert L. and Terry L. Bowen Laboratory
attributes.description: The Robert L. and Terry L. Bowen Laboratory was built in 2003. The building is used to test various infrastructures and materials against extreme conditions such as earthquakes, explosions, and  to research the behavior of large structural models in extreme events such as earthquakes, blasts, and major impacts. Key features of the structure include its large size, strong floor, and range of equipment. Research completed in the building aims to create more efficient and safe construction methods.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Bowen Laboratory was named in honor of Robert L. and Terry L. Bowen. Robert Bowen received a bachelor's degree in Civil Engineering from Purdue in 1962 and went on to found the Bowen Engineering Corporation. The Bowen's also provided a generous donation to the university that went towards the construction of this building.

attributes.Name: Lambert Field
attributes.description: Lambert Field was built in 1965 to house the baseball team after construction began on Mackey Arena. Before its construction, the Old Lambert Field, or Ross-Ade Field, was located on Northwestern Avenue next to this location. In 1999, the field began to go through yearly renovations including a new outfield wall, irrigation systems, new bullpens, and adjustments to the screens and fences to protect fans and cars. In 2012, the field was taken out of use and was replaced by Alexander Field.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The field was named after Ward "Piggy" Lambert who was a Purdue basketball coach for 29 years. Lambert was a legendary coach who pioneered the fast-break and coached many successful players including John Wooden.

attributes.Name: Rankin Track and Field Complex
attributes.description: The Rankin Track and Field complex was built in 1967 to house the Purdue track and field teams. The complex contains a 400-meter track, pole vault, high jump, long jump, and triple jump runways, press box, and an electronic scoreboard.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The track and field complex is named after Dave Rankin. Rankin was a Purdue track and field coach from 1947-1981 and football coach in 1947 and 1948. He received many honors including the Indiana Football Hall of Fame, Drake Relays Coaches Hall of Fame, and the Sports Illustrated Silver Anniversary Football All-American Award. Rankin was also a distinguished athlete and fighter pilot in the Marine Corps.

attributes.Name: Grand Stand
attributes.description: An addition was added to the grand stand in 1921.

attributes.Name: Grand Stand
attributes.description: A grand stand was built next to Stuart Field and the armory in 1900.

attributes.Name: American Railway Building
attributes.description: In 1997 an air conditioning unit was added to the American Railway building. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Married Student Courts Pavilion
attributes.description: The Married Student Courts Pavilion is located at squirrel park. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Married Student Courts Bathroom
attributes.description: The Married Students Courts Bathroom is a small structure located at Squirrel Park. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Sheep Barn
attributes.description: A small structure was built east of the Sheep Barn that was build in 1906. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Service Building
attributes.description: The Service Building was built on the south end of campus. The building was torn down in 2012 to make room for Lyles-Porter Hall.

attributes.Name: Mohawk Dormitories
attributes.description: The Mohawk Dormitories were 4 barracks style temporary dormitories that were built after World War II. These buildings were built by the Federal Public Housing Administration to accommodate the overflow of students after the war. On January 11, 1951 a fire destroyed part of one of  the Mohawk Temporary Dormitories. In 1954 all four of the temporary dormitories were removed.

attributes.Name: Iroquois Dormitories
attributes.description: The Iroquois Dormitories were 4 barracks style temporary dormitories that were built after World War II. These buildings were built by the Federal Public Housing Administration (FPHA) to accommodate the overflow of students after the war. All 4 of the temporary dormitories were removed in 1954.

attributes.Name: Beck Agricultural Center
attributes.description: The Beck Agricultural Center is located 5 miles northwest of the Purdue University, West Lafayette campus. The building was built in 2007 to house meetings and events for education and training in the field of agriculture. It contains multipurpose rooms and classrooms that can hold 10-250 guests.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building is named after Beck's Hybrids. Beck's Hybrids was founded by Lawrence Beck and his son Francis in 1937. Both Beck men, along with Francis's son Sonny, were Purdue Alumni. Beck's Hybrids has 12 locations and is also the largest family-owned seed retailer in the United States.

attributes.Name: John S. Wright Forestry Center
attributes.description: Located in the Martell Forest, the John S. Wright Forestry center houses research, teaching, and conference facilities for Purdue's Department of Forestry and Natural Resources. The building also contains two greenhouses. The Martell Forest sits in the Central Till Plain in Tippecanoe County. It is comprised of 477 acres and is located 7.5 miles west of the Purdue University West Lafayette campus.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building is named in honor of John Shepard Wright who graduated in from Purdue in 1892. In 1964, he made a generous donation to Department of Forestry and Natural Resources for the promotion of forestry in Indiana. Mr. Wright was a botanist, an Eli Lily executive, and a friend of many forestry leaders in Indiana.

attributes.Name: Elizabeth G. and William R. Wood Memorial Residence Hall
attributes.description: Originally named Women's Residence Hall West, the Elizabeth G. and William R. Wood Residence Hall is a 42 x 285 feet, three-story, brick, stone, and reinforced concrete structure. It contains 81 student rooms and houses 140 students. It also contains a kitchen, dining rooms, a manager's suite, lounges, a recreation room, and a laundry room. It was erected as a PWA project and was renamed Elizabeth G. and William R. Wood Memorial Residence Hall in 1969. It is now part of Windsor Residence Halls.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building was named after William R. Wood who donated a generous gift to the University and requested that an Elizabeth G. and William R. Memorial be established.

attributes.Name: Franklin Levering Cary Quadrangle (NE)
attributes.description: The Franklin Levering Cary Hall Northeast building was the second building built in the Cary Quadrangle. When it was built, the building had rooms for 116 students, all of which are furnished similar to the first building. It also contained lounges, a women's reception room, a manager's office, and living room suit, a dining room, and fully equipped kitchen. This building was originally intended to be a women's dormitory but, due to legislative issues with the land, construction was delayed until the decision was made that it would be more advantageous to build a men's dormitory. 3 more buildings were constructed to form the Cary Quadrangle. The entire quadrangle was remodeled during a six year renovation project from 2000 to 2006.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Frank and Jessie Levering Cary of Lafayette donated $50,000 to build the dormitory in memory of their son, Franklin Levering Cary. Franklin died suddenly of appendicitis shortly before his anticipated college enrollment date in 1912.

attributes.Name: Franklin Levering Cary Quadrangle (NW)
attributes.description: The Franklin Levering Cary Hall Northwest building was the fourth building built in the Cary Quadrangle. When it was built, this building had rooms for 116 students, all of which are furnished similar to the first three buildings. One more building was constructed to form the Cary Quadrangle in 1939. The entire quadrangle was remodeled during a six year renovation project from 2000 to 2006.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Frank and Jessie Levering Cary of Lafayette donated $50,000 to build the dormitory in memory of their son, Franklin Levering Cary. Franklin died suddenly of appendicitis shortly before his anticipated college enrollment date in 1912.

attributes.Name: Franklin Levering Cary Quadrangle (South)
attributes.description: The Franklin Levering Cary Hall South building was the fifth and final building built in the Cary Quadrangle. When it was built, this building had rooms for 400 students, all of which are furnished similar to the first four buildings. It also contained central offices for the manager, food supervisor, and executive housekeeper, women's reception rooms, lounge, four dining rooms, and two fully-equipped kitchens. The entire quadrangle was remodeled during a six year renovation project from 2000 to 2006.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Frank and Jessie Levering Cary of Lafayette donated $50,000 to build the dormitory in memory of their son, Franklin Levering Cary. Franklin died suddenly of appendicitis shortly before his anticipated college enrollment date in 1912.

attributes.Name: Horticultural Greenhouse
attributes.description: In 1996 all the greenhouses were torn down except for the main greenhouse building in order to make way for a new state of the art facility.

attributes.Name: Horticultural Greenhouse
attributes.description: A large addition was added to the remaining piece of the original Horticulture Greenhouse in 1998. This addition created a state of the art facility that serves the Department of Horticulture & Landscape Architecture.

attributes.Name: Aeronautical Engineering Building
attributes.description: The Aeronautical Engineering Building was erected in 1942 northeast of the Mechanical Engineering Building. It contained staff offices and aerodynamics and structures laboratories. In 1950, it was absorbed by the Mechanical Engineering Building and was designated as Unit 3 of the school of Mechanical and Aeronautical Engineering.

attributes.Name: Ross-Ade Stadium 1
attributes.description: A concession stand and two ticket booths were added south of Ross-Ade Stadium in 1968.

attributes.Name: Ross-Ade Stadium 2
attributes.description: A concession stand and two ticket booths were added south of Ross-Ade Stadium in 1968.

attributes.Name: Ross-Ade Stadium 3
attributes.description: A concession stand and two ticket booths were added south of Ross-Ade Stadium in 1968.

attributes.Name: Ross-Ade Stadium 6
attributes.description: In 1970, larger bleachers were installed south of the football field. This added 1,200 seats to the stadium and included handicapped-accessible seating.

attributes.Name: Ross-Ade Stadium 6
attributes.description: In 2014, the south end-zone bleachers were removed. A temporary patio was put in place while further plans were made.

attributes.Name: Ross-Ade Stadium Locker Room
attributes.description: The Ross-Ade Stadium Locker Room was constructed on the southwest corner of the stadium to provide meeting and dressing areas for entire football teams. When the original locker rooms were constructed in Ross-Ade stadium in 1924 they were only made to accommodate 33 players and several coaches. When this locker room was constructed, teams had 80-100 players with multiple coaches and medical staff. The building included locker and shower facilities, a toilet room, a training room, and a medical office. The locker room is also used for visiting track and baseball teams. The cost of constructing this locker room as well as remodeling the home team locker room under the East stands of the stadium was $554,000.

attributes.Name: Latino Cultural Center
attributes.description: The Latino Cultural Center was moved to 426 Waldron Street from its previous location at 600 N. Russell Street in 2017. The Latino Cultural Center strives to improve awareness and understanding of the Latino Culture and provides a space for Latino students to celebrate their culture and share their experiences. The building contains a lounge, study room, conference room, computer lab, kitchen, and volleyball court.

attributes.Name: Asian American and Asian Resource and Cultural Center
attributes.description: The Asian American and Asian Resource and Cultural Center was moved to 915 5th Street in 2016 from its previous location in the Stewart Center. The center provides education and support for a diverse population of students on the Purdue Campus. The building contains a lounge, kitchen, conference room, computer lab, exhibition space, and storage for student organizations.

attributes.Name: Native American Educational and Cultural Center
attributes.description: The Native American Educational and Cultural Center was moved from the South Campus Courts to 903 Fifth Street in 2016. The center provides education about Indigenous cultures and a community space for students, faculty, and staff from over 45 tribal nations. The building contains a conference room, computer lab, multi-purpose room, and student lounge.

attributes.Name: First Street Towers Eastern
attributes.description: This structure is part of the First Street Towers complex that was designed with upperclassmen in mind. These towers have single air-conditioned rooms with private baths are arranged in clusters of no more than 22 students around a central living room/dinette area. The total cost of constructing the East and Central towers was $52,000,000.

attributes.Name: First Street Towers Western
attributes.description: The structure is the third building of the First Street Towers residence halls. The western First Street Towers building faces the eastern building. The First Street Towers have single air-conditioned rooms with private baths are arranged in clusters of no more than 22 students around a central living room/dinette area. The building was designed with upperclassmen in mind and included input from residents during the initial planning stages.

attributes.Name: Farm Residence
attributes.description: The Farm Residence was built on the Purdue University farm but the original start date is unknown. The Farm Residence was the residence of the Dean of Agriculture, Dean John H. Skinner, for many years. In 1925, Dean Skinner was asked to vacated the residence so it could be repaired and rebuilt. The Residence was eventually torn down in 1958.

attributes.Name: Golf Starter House
attributes.description: An experimental, thin, shell educational type structure was constructed to be used as a second golf starter house. It was later removed in 1999.

attributes.Name: Pharmacy
attributes.description: Construction of a new pharmacy building was completed in 1930. Upon completion the structure was 52 x 136 foot in dimensions and three stories in height. The building was composed of dark tapestry brick, reinforced concrete, and trimmed with Indiana limestone in the windows and entrances. A red tile roof which was complemented by several small dormers and two ventilating cupolas. The Pharmacy building contained a complete drug store, three offices, three lecture rooms, a library, and 23 laboratories, including a radiological laboratory. The building name changed to the Geosciences Building in 1970.  In 1987 construction began to incorporate the building into the new Helen B. Schleman Hall of Student Services.

attributes.Name: University Library
attributes.description: In 1954 the University Library Annex was torn down in order to make room for a large addition to the library. When the addition was added the library became the Purdue Memorial Center (later known as the Stewart Center).

attributes.description: Hangar No. 7 is located on the Purdue University Airport. The hangar was constructed by the Purdue Research Foundation at an approximate cost of $1,183,000. After construction, the hangar was leased to Lafayette Aviation.

attributes.Name: Federal Aviation Agency (FAA) Tower
attributes.description: The Federal Aviation Agency (FAA) Tower is located on the Purdue University Airport, southwest of Hangar No. 4. The building was funded by the federal government and was expected to cost $200,000. Before the permanent tower was built, a temporary mobile tower was proposed to only be used on Saturdays when home football games were played.

attributes.description: The High Pressure Laboratory Annex is located on the Zucrow Laboratories Complex, west of the High Pressure Research Laboratory. The building contains a turbine lab, fabrication shop, process mechanics room, laser lab, four test cells, and two control rooms.

attributes.description: The World War II Temporary Buildings are located north of the Chemical Engineering and Physics Building. These buildings were built to accommodate the influx of students after World War II.

attributes.Name: Student Army Training Corps (SATC) Buildings
attributes.description: The Student Army Training Corps (SATC) Buildings were built near the later site of the Mechanical Engineering Building and Engineering Mall. The buildings were built to accommodate the influx of students after World War I.

attributes.Name: Land O'Lakes Center for Experiential Learning and Purina Pavilion
attributes.description: The Land O'Lakes Center for Experiential Learning and Purina Pavilion was built in 2017. It contains the Boilermaker Butcher Block and research and teaching spaces for meat and protein sciences. The building also contains spaces for informational events on livestock management. The building was built alongside the Hobart and Russell Creighton Hall of Animal Sciences at a total cost of $60 million.

attributes.Name: Farm Residence
attributes.description: The Farm Cottage was one of the first buildings to be built on campus. It was a brick residence that was first occupied by Professor J. S. Hougham. It was later occupied by the farm superintendent and was torn down in 1928 to make room for a new farm residence for the Dean of Agriculture.

attributes.Name: Boiler and Gas House
attributes.description: The Boiler and Gas House, also referred to as the Engine House, was built to generate steam, gas, and water for the surrounding buildings. The building contained an engine, large steam boilers, and force-pump which provided heating and lighting to nearby buildings. On July 16, 1877, a fire occurred in the Boiler and Gas House and the building was repaired for $750. The building was torn down in 1904 and replaced with the new Power Plant that was built next to the Electrical Engineering Building.

attributes.Name: Military Hall
attributes.description: Military Hall was built in 1874 and was originally used as a drill hall.

attributes.Name: Peirce Conservatory
attributes.description: The original Peirce Conservatory and Greenhouse was built directly west of Ladies Hall. The greenhouse was about 50 x 20 ft with an addition for boiler and fuel, and for potting purposes. Samples from the garden were donated to the Botanical Collection. In 1906 the greenhouse was no longer practical to be repaired. Because of this, a new green house was built in the same location in 1907. In 1921 it was moved behind Stanley Coulter Hall from its original location on the corner of State Street and University Street. It was moved again in 1927 to to a building next door.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The greenhouse was named after Martin L. Peirce, a Purdue Trustee and the Treasurer of the Board of Trustees, who donated the money to be used for the purposes of a conservatory.

attributes.Name: Experimental Feeding Barn
attributes.description: The Experimental Feeding barn was completed in 1890. When it was built, the structure was 60 x 40 feet with two projections. One projection contained offices and was used for weighing purposes. The other projection contained the engine room, silos, granary, and cutting and grinding machinery.

attributes.Name: Cattle Barn
attributes.description: The Cattle Barn was built in 1919. It was an A-frame structure made of stucco, tile, clay, and concrete. The main portion of the barn was 98 by 65 feet and had two attached wings that were 68 by 34 feet. The building contained stalls, storage and feed rooms, a grain elevator, grinding machinery, and scales. It was also known as the Beef Cattle Barn and was one of two cattle barns on campus at the time.

attributes.Name: Peirce Conservatory
attributes.description: In 1907  new Peirce Conservatory and Greenhouse was built directly west of Ladies Hall in place of the old conservatory that was torn down. In 1921 it was moved behind Stanley Coulter hall from its original location on the corner of State street and University street.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The greenhouse was named after Martin L. Peirce, a Purdue Trustee and the Treasurer of the Board of Trustees. Mr. Peirce earned a salary while serving as the treasurer of the University but donated it all to build and maintain the Pierce Conservatory.

attributes.Name: Science Hall
attributes.description: In 1903 an addition was added to the Mechanical Laboratory (Mechanic's Hall) and it was renamed Science Hall. It consisted of a two-story brick front building with two wings, and housed the departments of Biology and Chemistry. The front and west wing were devoted to chemistry and included a lecture room with adjoining preparation room; three laboratories for general chemistry and qualitative analysis, quantitative analysis, and advanced work; three private laboratories; two balance rooms; a supply room; a furnace room; a spectroscope and polarimeter room; the department library and offices. The east wing contained the office, laboratories, lecture room, collections and store room of the Biology department.

attributes.Name: Civil Engineering Building
attributes.description: The Civil Engineering Building was built in 1906. It contained two main floors and an attic story.

attributes.Name: Poultry Husbandry
attributes.description: The Poultry Husbandry building was built in 1924.

attributes.Name: Forney Hall of Chemical Engineering
attributes.description: Construction of the Chemical Engineering building was completed in 1939.

attributes.Name: Peirce Conservatory
attributes.description: Peirce Conservatory was moved from behind Stanley Coulter Hall to a building next door in 1928. It was built at a combined cost of $16,500 with the Small Animal House. It contained a head house, two greenhouse wings, an animal house wing, three laboratories, and a small greenhouse for diseased plants.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The greenhouse was named after Martin L. Peirce, a Purdue Trustee and the Treasurer of the Board of Trustees. Mr. Peirce earned a salary while serving as the treasurer of the University but donated it all to build and maintain the Pierce Conservatory.

attributes.Name: Purdue Memorial Union
attributes.description: Phase two of the construction of the Purdue Memorial Union began in 1929.

attributes.Name: Agricultural Chemistry Building
attributes.description: The Agricultural Chemistry Building was built in 1938. It contained the offices of the State Chemist and his staff, a library, 19 laboratories, and four cold storage rooms.

attributes.Name: Oliver Perkins Terry House
attributes.description: Located at 608 Waldron Street, the Oliver Perkins Terry house operated as a dormitory unit at the discretion of the trustees of the university. It was previously the Theta Chi Fraternity house until it was purchased by the Purdue Research Foundation for $32,500 in 1937. The house was to be a memorial of Dr. Oliver Perkins Terry, the former head of the university student health service. It was sold back to the Purdue Research Foundation in 1959 for $100,000 and was given to Acacia Fraternity in exchange for property on state street. The  Dining Lounge Center Building in the Gable Courts (Terry Courts) was built in 1957 and took on the Oliver Perkins Terry House name in 1961.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Mrs. Geraldine Terry (widow of the late Dr. 0. P. Terry) desired to provide by donation a suitable memorial at or in connection with Purdue University to her late husband, Oliver Perkins Terry. She donated $30,000 and asked that the property owned by the research foundation on 608 Waldron street be named after her late husband.

attributes.Name: Physics Building
attributes.description: The Physics Building was constructed in 1941. When it was built, it contained staff offices, laboratories, dark rooms, workshops, a cyclotron, several lecture rooms, and the Charles B. Stuart Laboratory of Applied Physics.

attributes.Name: South Campus Courts - Phase 1
attributes.description: In 1954 the first two Student Memorial Union Courts buildings were built along with the Student Union B Courts (State Street Courts). They provided housing for 800 men, which was a small portion of of the anticipated increased student population. The Student Memorial Union Courts and Student Union B Courts were built at a combined cost of approximately $1,300,000. They were completely self-financed and were located 3 blocks south of the Union. Six more buildings were added to the area shortly after and were also referred to as the Student Memorial Union Courts. All of the buildings were later referred to as the Harrison Street Courts before being renamed the South Campus Courts in 1965. In 1994 the two original buildings were removed and replaced with a parking lot.

attributes.Name: Purdue University Student Health Center
attributes.description: When the Purdue University Student Health Center was built, it provided beds for over 90 patients. It also contained other health facilities for surgeries, x-rays, psychiatric services, physiotherapy, cystoscopy, and electroencephalography. The health center also consists of a central supply room, fracture room, emergency room, cafeteria, and kitchen for both in-patients and out-patients requiring special diets. It was originally called the Student Hospital and was renamed the Student Health Center in 1991.

attributes.Name: Slayter Center of Performing Arts
attributes.description: The Slayter Center of Performing Arts began as a multipurpose structure with an outdoor stage and all season utility. The exterior design featured an 85 foot high steel tripod that suspended a 200 ton concrete roof over a 63x43 foot stage. The building was designed to look like Stonehenge in Wiltshire, England and had a "flaring horn" design that compressed and projected sound instead of just reflecting it. It's walls were made of stelae which is similar to the stone monoliths that make up Stonehenge. In between the stones is broken yellow french glass that is held together with black epoxy-resin. When it was constructed, a small pool was built in front which could be drained and used for dancing or as an orchestra pit.
attributes.dedicationinfo: In 1963, Dr. R. Games and Marie Slayter donated $300,000 to Purdue University for the construction of Slayter Center for the Performing Arts. A 1921 Purdue graduate in chemical engineering, Dr. Slayter was also a member of the Purdue Marching Band. He was also the former president of research and development at Owens-Corning and was most noted for inventing fiberglass.

attributes.Name: Education Building
attributes.description: The Chemistry department was moved from Science Hall into the Chemistry Building in 1907. The building had three floors with an attic. It contained chemistry laboratories, lecture rooms, classrooms, preparation rooms, stock rooms, a library, a dark room, and offices. Due to the expansion of the chemistry department, a new Chemistry building (the current Richard Benbridge Wetherill Lab of Chemistry) was built in 1930. The Chemistry Building was called the Education building starting in the 1930s because the education department moved into the building. The building was torn down in 1990 to make room for Steven C. Beering Hall of Liberal Arts and Education.

attributes.Name: U.S. Experiment Station Annex
attributes.description: The U.S. Experiment Station Annex was built in 1900. It was used for teaching Farm Mechanics and Farm Implements. It contained a large lecture hall that accommodated Winter Courses in Agriculture, larger classes, and judging exercises. The building was torn down in 1907 and its materials were used to construct the Agricultural Experiment Station Seed House (now known as the Forestry Building).

attributes.Name: Mechanical Engineering Building
attributes.description: The Mechanical Engineering building was rebuilt after the original building burned down in 1894. It had a three story front with a clock tower at the center and rear portion with extensive working laboratories.

attributes.Name: Power Plant
attributes.description: The second Power Plant was built in 1904. It held four 250-(hp) boilers and one 75-(kv.a.) engine driven generator. The new Power Plant was built to replace the Gas and Boiler House (also known as the engine house) that was built in 1974. In 1909, a boiler was added and the general equipment increased with a purchase of a new 225-(kv.a.) engine-driven generator. This was sustainable for less than five years and, in 1912, another boiler was added to this plant. It became inadequate to meet the needs of the university and was replaced by the North Heating and Power Plant that was built in 1925.

attributes.Name: Gymnasium
attributes.description: In 1901 a small addition was added to Military Hall. This addition added a bath room and heating to the gymnasium. The total cost of the addition was $724 ($473 for general construction and $251 for heating and plumbing).

attributes.Name: Baptist Church
attributes.description: This structure is the Baptist church that was on the corner of Columbia and Chauncey. No other information is currently available regarding this structure including exact start and end dates. This structure only appeared on Purdue's Map in a 1903 Y.M.C.A campus handbook.

attributes.Name: M.E. Church
attributes.description: This structure is the Methodist church that was on the corner of Chauncey and South Street. No other information is currently available regarding this structure including exact start and end dates. This structure only appeared on Purdue's Map in a 1903 Y.M.C.A campus handbook.

attributes.Name: Ticket Office
attributes.description: The ticket office, built in 1902, replaced an old ticket office that was unattractive and flimsy. The Class of 1902 collected money for the erection of the new ticket office.

attributes.Name: Agricultural Administration Building
attributes.description: At its opening the new Agricultural Experiment Station Building was two stories high with a basement. It was constructed using brick, stone trimmings, a tile roof, reinforced concrete floors, iron and slate stairs, and utilized fireproof construction throughout. When it was built, it was one of the largest buildings on campus and many deemed it one of the best buildings in the United States to be devoted exclusively to experiment station work. The new structure replaced the functions of the old experiment station that was torn down in 1907. During its history, this building underwent multiple renovations and name changes and was renamed the Agricultural Administration Building in 1969.

attributes.Name: Felix Haas Hall
attributes.description: Originally called the Memorial Gymnasium, Felix Haas Hall was built in 1908. The building was constructed in memory of those who died in the Indianapolis train wreck of October 31, 1903 that killed football team members and fans. When it was built, the gymnasium consisted of a basketball court, indoor track, gymnasium, a swimming pool, 35 adjoined shower-baths, and 1800 lockers. The gymnasium was the headquarters for physical education for men and intercollegiate athletics until the completion of the Lambert Fieldhouse in the late 1930s. The building was converted into the Computer Science building in 1985.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Memorial Gymnasium was dedicated to the lives lost in the Purdue Special accident on October 31, 1903. The seventeen steps of the building commemorate their lives. A substantial part of the funding for the building was a result of a generous donation from the Big Four Railroad. On December 1, 2006 the building was renamed in honor of Felix Haas, the former head of the Division of Mathematical Sciences, Dean of the School of Science, and University Provost.

attributes.Name: Wagon Shed
attributes.description: The Wagon Shed was located in between the livestock judging pavilion (now the Grounds Service Building) and the Horse Barn (now Herrick Laboratories).

attributes.Name: Hog House
attributes.description: The Hog House was built in 1910 and was located south of where the Veterinary Complex stands today. It was a modern piggery, arranged for experimental feeding and breeding of swine.

attributes.Name: Agricultural Experiment Station Seed House
attributes.description: The Agricultural Experiment Station Seed House was constructed from 1907-1910. It was constructed using materials from the old experiment station that was torn down in 1907.

attributes.Name: Entomology Environment Laboratory
attributes.description: The Service Greenhouse was built in 1910 and was used for the Experiment Station. It was two stories high  30 x 54 feet. In 1962, its name changed to the Entomology Environmental Lab because it started to house the Department of Entomology instead of the Department of Botany and Plant Pathology.

attributes.Name: Poultry House
attributes.description: The Poultry House was built in 1911 on the Schwegler land. It was used by the poultry department and contained laboratories and offices.

attributes.Name: Hen House
attributes.description: Two Hen Houses were located on the Purdue poultry farm west of the Poultry Husbandry building. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Michael Golden Engineering Laboratories and Shops
attributes.description: The Practical Mechanics Building that was constructed in 1910. When it was built, the building covered 43,000 square feet and could house up to 350 students at a time.
attributes.dedicationinfo: "On November 20, 1921 a bronze tablet was put in place bearing the inscription 'This building has been officially named Michael Golden Shops to commemorate the life of one who from 1884 to 1917 devoted himself untiringly to the university and its students.'"

attributes.Name: Steer Barn
attributes.description: The Steer Barn was built in 1911 and contained lots and sheds that were used for the experimental feeding of steers.

attributes.Name: Smith Hall
attributes.description: Smith Hall was built in 1913 in order to meet the growing need of the School of Agriculture. The building was made of brick, stone, reinforced concrete floors, and a tile roof. When it was built, it consisted of a two story front part that was 60 x 120 feet, a rear 72 x 118 feet portion, and a connecting building that was 23 x 30 feet. The building contained offices, lecture rooms, private laboratories, a commercial creamery, locker rooms, toilet rooms, and rooms for making butter, ice cream and cheese.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Smith Hall was built using money donated by William C. Smith of Williamsport, Indiana. Before this generous donation he also gave the university wilderness land in Minnesota. Smith Hall was the third building that was funded by a single individual aside from the 6 original Purdue Buildings that were funded mostly through John Purdue. The other two were Fowler Hall and Heavilon Hall.

attributes.Name: University Library
attributes.description: The original free-standing library of Purdue University was built in 1913.

attributes.Name: Sheep Barn
attributes.description: The new Sheep Barn was used for the breeding and feeding of sheep.

attributes.Name: Brooder House
attributes.description: The Brooder House was built in 1914. It was 100 by 14 feet and was built over an incubator cellar. It also contained incubators, egg testing rooms, brooders, hovers, and laboratories. The building was used for research in testing and handling eggs.

attributes.Name: Veterinary Animal Isolation Building 1
attributes.description: The Veterinary Animal Isolation Building - 1 was constructed to house animals undergoing treatment. When it was built, it was a one-story frame building about 300 feet long with pens accommodating about 400 hogs. It was formerly known as the serum plant and serum hog house. The total cost of constructing this building, the Rendering Plant, and Hyper barn was $27,346.

attributes.Name: Stanley Coulter Hall
attributes.description: Construction of Stanley Coulter Hall was completed in 1917.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building was named for Stanley Coulter who joined the Purdue faculty in 1887. He was the first dean of the School of Science in 1907 and the first dean of Men in 1919. He served in those positions and was a longtime chairman of the faculy until his retirement in 1926.

attributes.Name: Bell House
attributes.description: The original Bell House was located south of Stuart Field and east of the Armory. In 1939, it was moved between Ross-Ade Stadium and Cary Quadrangle. The bell from the Bell House was originally taken to the home games; however, after two attempts at stealing the bell, the bell was only brought out after games. The bell from the Bell House is now rung after every Big Ten home football game victory. The bell is currently taken care of by the Gimlet Club.

attributes.Name: Serum Laboratory
attributes.description: The original Serum Laboratory that was built in 1913 to create a serum to prevent hog cholera. It was renamed the Postmortem Laboratory in 1943.

attributes.Name: Hog Shed
attributes.description: The Hog Shed was built in 1916 and was located southwest of the livestock judging pavilion. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Sheds
attributes.description: The sheds were located south of the Livestock Judging Pavilion and the Steer Barn. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Horticultural Greenhouse
attributes.description: The Horticultural Greenhouse was built in 1915. The greenhouse units were able to be adapted for different growing conditions (hot, cold, humid, etc.) and there was 16,000 square feet of growing space. It also had four detached houses connected by a service house and corridor.

attributes.Name: Armory
attributes.description: The current armory was built in the same location as the armory that burned down in 1916. When it was built, the Armory housed the Army, Air Force, and Navy ROTC Battalions. It also consisted of 3 classrooms, offices, and a large drill deck shed complete with a rifle range. The All-American Marching Band also houses the Big Bass Drum in the Armory. On January 13, 1928, a fire broke out in the oil store room and ignited the wooden sheeting on the northern end of the roof. The fire worked its way southward along the roof until roofing tiles dropped to the floor below. The fire also damaged the northern wall of the Armory.

attributes.Name: Horse Barn
attributes.description: The Horse Barn was erected to "replace the barn which was destroyed by fire in 1911." It was a brick structure with concrete floors and a tile roof. The front part, or main barn, was two stories high and 94x41 feet. Two one-story wings extended back from either end of the main part and were 82x39 feet. Between the wings was a well-lighted Judging Pavilion with tan-bark floor. The building contained feed rooms, wash rooms, an office, 28 single stalls, 12 double stalls, and accommodated 40 to 50 horses.

attributes.Name: Marriott Hall
attributes.description: Marriott Hall was built in 2010 for the department of hospitality and tourism management. The building contains the Lavazza bistro, a demonstration kitchen, classrooms, offices, and a reception area. The building is a LEED Silver accredited building and is the first of its kind on campus.
attributes.dedicationinfo: On April 17, 2012 Marriott Hall held its dedication which was lead by Purdue President France A. Cordova. The building is named after J. Willard and Alice S. Marriott whose foundation donated $4 million towards the construction of Marriott Hall.

attributes.Name: Mechanical Engineering
attributes.description: The old Mechanical Engineering building was added onto in 1921.

attributes.Name: Matthews Hall
attributes.description: Matthews Hall, originally the Home Economics Building, is located to the southwest end of Oval Drive. It was constructed in 1921 using brick and stone and was used for Home Economics courses. It was renamed Home Economics Two when Stone Hall was built in 1954. In March of 1972,  a substantial fire occurred on the second floor that required a renovation. The building was renamed Matthews Hall in November 1976.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building was renamed Matthews Hall in November, 1976 after the Dean of the school of Home Economics Mary L. Matthews, who laid the foundations for the school of Home Economics.

attributes.Name: Physical Plant Garage and Storage
attributes.description: The Physical Plant Garage and Storage building was located east of the North Heating and Power Plant. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Locomotive Museum 2
attributes.description: The locomotives from the old locomotive museum were moved into a newer building 1923. The locomotives in the exhibit include an 8-wheel engine, a camel-back type locomotive, the Daniel Nason locomotive, several models of locomotives and cylinders, and a New England stage coach-passenger car.

attributes.Name: Repair Shop
attributes.description: The Repair Shop was located west of the Horse and Sheep Barn.

attributes.Name: Student Union Memorial
attributes.description: The first phase of construction of the Purdue Memorial Union commenced in 1922. It was originally built using grayish red brick, Bedford stone trimming, and dark slate roofing. The overall design was inspired by the American Gothic architecture movement.

attributes.Name: Ross-Ade Stadium
attributes.description: Ross-Ade football stadium was constructed in 1924. When it was first built, it had a 13,500 person seating capacity and standing room for an additional 5,000 people in the north end of the stadium.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Ross-Ade Stadium was dedicated on November 22, 1924, in a game against Purdue's rival Indiana University. The Boilermakers won the game 26-7. The stadium was named after David E. Ross and George Ade. Ross and Ade donated 65-acres of land to build the stadium on. Ross also conceived the idea for the Stadium and was a president on the Board of Trustees. Ade was also a playwright and humorist.

attributes.Name: Power Plant Number 2
attributes.description: The North Power plant was constructed from 1923-1925 in order to meet the growing needs of the University. It supplied the university's buildings with light and power in the most economically responsible way.

attributes.Name: Horticulture Building
attributes.description: The Horticulture Building was constructed in 1926.

attributes.Name: Peirce Conservatory
attributes.description: In 1921 the Pierce conservatory was moved behind Stanley Coulter Hall from its original location on the corner of State Street and University Street. It was used for instruction in Botany and for propagating plants for the Campus. It was moved again in 1927 to a building next door.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The greenhouse was named after Martin L. Peirce, a Purdue Trustee and the Treasurer of the Board of Trustees, who donated the money to be used for the purposes of a conservatory.

attributes.Name: Forestry Building
attributes.description: An addition to the Agricultural Experiment Station Annex was constructed in 1926. The addition included adding a three-story 46 by 68 addition to the existing building. The building contained several offices of the Department of Agricultural Extension and the freight and an express receiving office of the University.

attributes.Name: Service Building & Greenhouse
attributes.description: One 125 x 135 foot unit was added to the Horticulture Greenhouse in 1924. It was built to accommodate increasing needs for research space in the fields of Entomology and Horticulture.

attributes.Name: Student Services Annex- One
attributes.description: The Student Services Annex - One was originally called Chemical Engineering Unit-one. It changed names multiple times until it was torn down in 2008 to make room for the west portion of the current Mechanical Engineering Building.

attributes.Name: Poultry Husbandry
attributes.description: An addition to the Poultry Husbandry Building was completed in 1928. It included the addition of a 54 x 70 foot two-story structure that was made of brick, stone and reinforced concrete. It added two small laboratories and a pavilion.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Harriet O. Fowler gifted approximately 800 acres of land in Benton County to Purdue University. The land was intended to be sold and the proceeds were to be used for a residence hall for men named after James. M. Fowler, Junior.

attributes.Name: Agricultural Engineering Building
attributes.description: A new Agricultural Engineering building was built due west of the horticulture building. When it was built, it contained seven laboratories, four offices, a tool room, and a locker room.

attributes.Name: Civil Engineering (Grissom)
attributes.description: An addition was added to the original Civil Engineering building in 1928.

attributes.Name: Service & Stores
attributes.description: The Service and Stores building was constructed in 1929. It contained three offices, a drafting room, three shops, one garage, and three store rooms. At the time it was built, the Physical Plant and Stores Division of the Purchasing Department were housed in this building.

attributes.Name: Chemistry (New)
attributes.description: The first unit of a new Chemistry Building was built in 1930. The building was constructed in installments because the cost of the construction was too great for the university in 1928.

attributes.Name: Mechanical Engineering Building
attributes.description: The first portion of the New Mechanical Engineering building was completed in 1931.

attributes.Name: Service Building & Greenhouse
attributes.description: Another 125 x 35 foot unit was added to the Horticulture Greenhouse in 1928.

attributes.Name: Peirce Conservatory
attributes.description: In 1933, the Peirce Conservatory was remodeled and a major addition was added.

attributes.Name: Mechanical Engineering Building
attributes.description: The second unit of the of the mechanical engineering building was constructed in 1933.

attributes.Name: Small Animal House
attributes.description: The Small Animal House was built to house the large number of small animals, rats, guinea pigs, and rabbits used for work in animal nutrition. These animals were previously occupying space in the Veterinary building. The building was an A-frame building that was 50 feet long and 40 feet wide and was built near the present Veterinary plant. The Building was torn down in 1959 to make room for the new Holding Pen and Avian Isolation Units 1-9.

attributes.Name: University Library
attributes.description: Two wings were added to the original library in 1934.

attributes.Name: Service & Stores
attributes.description: A one story unit was added to the east end of the Service and Stores Building in 1933. This addition removed business offices from University Hall and other buildings where classes and teaching facilities were held.  After this addition, in 1937, the building was rented to the Soil Conservation Committee.

attributes.Name: Purdue Memorial Union
attributes.description: The Purdue Memorial Union was added onto in 1936. This addition expanded the building to the west and north and expanded the existing ballroom. The new east wing faced Grant street and contained a browsing library, student activity rooms, music rooms, a bowling alley, game room, and lounging grill. This addition also expanded the basement of the Union.

attributes.Name: Horticulture Building
attributes.description: An addition to the Horticulture Building was constructed in 1938. The building reopened on September 8, 1938 after the addition was completed.

attributes.Name: Physics
attributes.description: The original Physics Building was constructed in 1905. This portion of the building was torn down in 1990.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building was dedicated to the Physics department in January of 1905.

attributes.Name: Niswonger Aviation Technology Building
attributes.description: The Niswonger Aviation Technology Building was built in 1934. The facility originally housed airport operations and administration facilities and was added onto in 1941. The building also housed the plane used by Amelia Earhart during her last flight in 1937.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Niswonger Aviation Technology Building is named after Scott Niswonger. Niswonger received a degree in Aviation Technology in 1968 and made a generous donation towards the expansion of the Aviation Technology Building.

attributes.Name: Men's Residence Hall Annex A
attributes.description: The Men's Residence Hall Annex A was acquired from Alpha Xi Delta sorority in 1938 for $22,500. The building provided additional residence facilities for twenty men. The house was operated in conjunction with the Franklin Levering Cary Quadrangle West Hall under the direction of the Men's Residence Halls. In 1946, the building was maintained as a dormitory for women and as an infirmary. In 1948, the annexes could no longer be used for student housing because the placement of fire escapes was too expensive.

attributes.Name: Service Building & Greenhouse
attributes.description: Two greenhouse units were added to the Horticulture Greenhouse in 1941. The greenhouses were built to be used for research on destructive tomato diseases.

attributes.Name: Cattle Barn
attributes.description: An addition was added to the Experimental Feeding barn in 1944. The addition included lots and sheds especially designed for the experimental steer feeding. After the addition, the building became a two-story frame structure, 35 by 43 feet, with wings 33 by 210 feet and 22 by 112 feet. The barn was used by the Agricultural Experiment station for the experimental feeding of cattle and sheep.

attributes.Name: Naval Science Building
attributes.description: The Naval Science Building was constructed at the request of the Navy. The Navy requested facilities at the university after the establishment of the Navy ROTC program. The building was demolished in order to build the Robert E. Heine Pharmacy Building.

attributes.Name: Aerospace Science Lab (Hangar No. 3)
attributes.description: Constructed in 1946, the Aerospace Science Lab, formerly known as Hangar No. 3,  is an aeronautical engineering laboratory and hangar. The Aerospace Sciences laboratory contains four wind tunnels (the Boeing Wind Tunnel and three smaller low-speed wind tunnels), a vacuum technology lab, and plasma and flow visualization lab.

attributes.Name: University Infirmary
attributes.description: The University Infirmary was part of the Bunker Hill dormitories (including the center Seneca dormitory) that were originally Bachelor Officers' Quarters (B.O.Q.'s) and barracks located at the Bunker Hill Naval Air Station in Peru, Indiana (now Grissom Air Reserve Base). They were relocated to Purdue University to fill the need for additional living quarters and classroom facilities. This building was located north of Cary hall, had a capacity of 85, and was used as an infirmary. The total cost of relocating all of the Bunker Hill dormitories was $234,589.07.

attributes.Name: Federal Public Housing Authority (FPHA) Housing Areas A, B, C, D
attributes.description: The Federal Public Housing Authority (FPHA) Housing Areas A, B, C, D were temporary houses that were built to meet the growing need of the university after World War II. Female enrollment largely increased between 1944-1945 leading to overcrowding at the university. After the war, many students were also now married and wanted to live with their families. This made grouping of students into dormitories more difficulty and increased the need for apartments at the university. The Federal Public Housing Authority (FPHA) agreed to provide 180 buildings (20 by 100 feet each) to accommodate both married and single students at a cost of approximately $350,000. This provided sanitary, power, and water facilities for these dormitory accommodations. These dwellings were located on University farm land on the south side of State Road 26 including both sides of Airport Road, the wooded area west of the Poultry Building, and on the intramural field.

attributes.Name: Experimental Rental Housing
attributes.description: The Experimental Rental Housing was comprised of 150 temporary hoses built on the south side of State Road 26 west of the University campus. The total cost of building all 150 houses was $400,000. These homes were used for Married Students and Staff Members. These temporary houses were built to meet the growing need of the university after World War II. Female enrollment largely increased between 1944-1945 leading to overcrowding at the university. After the war many students were also now married and wanted to live with their families. This made the grouping of students into dormitories more difficult and increased the need for apartments at the university.

attributes.Name: University Library Annex
attributes.description: A small temporary structure was built west of the Library in 1947. It was connected to the library and added 200 seats to give some relief to the university library.

attributes.Name: FWA 8
attributes.description: The FWA 8 building was built as part of the Federal Works Administration (FWA) project where pre-engineered buildings were brought to Purdue.
