These building were left over from World War II and were remodeled to be used as lecture halls, classrooms, and laboratories for the growing student body. Over the years, the buildings were used as chemistry and physics classrooms and laboratories, Naval Science and civil engineering spaces, the office for veterans administration, and as warehouses, before becoming the home of the Creative Arts department. This building was eventually torn down in 1987.

attributes.Name: Life Science Plant and Soils Laboratory
attributes.description: Originally called the head house, this building was built with the life science building (now the Lily Hall of Life Sciences), the Life Science Ranges, and the Life Science Animal Building. It originally housed the Departments of Biological Science, Animal Husbandry, Botany, and Plant Pathology and Agronomy. The building was renamed the The Life Science Plant and Soils Laboratory in 1952.

attributes.Name: Virginia C. Meredith Residence Hall
attributes.description: Originally called Men's Residence Hall X, the Virginia C. Meredith Residence Hall is an 'X' shaped building which provides accommodations for 604 co-ed students in 302 double rooms. It contains three 80 foot lounges, several study nooks in each wing (which were originally used for dates between students), six movie lounges in which students can watch films rented from the front office, and the preparatory kitchen for the Purdue residence hall dining services.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The residence hall was named after Virginia Claypool Meredith (1848-1936). She died at the age of 88 after a long career in the fields of agriculture and home economics. Mrs. Meredith earned the title of "Queen of American Agriculture" because of her support of farmers and farm life. In 1921, she became the first woman to serve as a trustee of Purdue University.

attributes.Name: Materials and Structural Testing Laboratories Building
attributes.description: The first unit of the Materials and Structural Testing Laboratories was built in 1952. This structure was one-story tall with a basement and was used as a materials testing lab and structures lab.

attributes.Name: Lilly Hall of Life Sciences
attributes.description: The Lilly Hall of Life Sciences originally housed the Departments of Biological Science, Animal Husbandry, Botany, and Plant Pathology and Agronomy. When it was built, it was the largest single academic structure on campus. Construction started with the west wing in 1951 and, in 1955, Agronomy moved into the building. Construction on the main entrance began in 1957 and Biology and Animal Sciences moved into the east wing in 1959. It was renamed Lilly Hall of Life Sciences in 1960 and in 1967 the basement was constructed and the building was remodeled.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Lilly Hall of Life Sciences was dedicated on December 14, 1960 in honor of Mr. Eli Lilly and Mr. J. K. Lilly. There was a luncheon this day in order for the Board of Trustees to meet these donors.

attributes.Name: South Campus Courts - Phase 3
attributes.description: The last South Campus Courts Building was built just east of the South Campus Court Building A. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Winthrop E. Stone Hall
attributes.description: Originally called the Home Economics Administration Building, it was renamed Winthrop E. Stone Hall in November, 1976.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building is named after Winthrop E. Stone, a former president of Purdue.  Dr. Stone was honored for the work he did to help establish and strengthen Purdue.

attributes.Name: Poultry Science Annex
attributes.description: The Poultry Science Annex was attached to the Poultry Science Building. When it was built it was "one of the best equipped in the nation for teaching and research work." The total construction cost of building the Poultry Science Building and Annex was $370,000.

attributes.Name: Poultry Science Building
attributes.description: The Poultry Science Building was located on the south side of State Street, immediately west of the Life Science Building. When it was built, this building contained "extensive research laboratories, staff offices, a department library, and a seminar and conference room." It replaced the function of the old Poultry Husbandry Building that was converted into the Harriett O. and James M. Fowler Jr. Memorial House. The poultry products annex (later known as the poultry science annex) was attached to this building and the total construction cost of both buildings was $370,000.

attributes.Name: Harvey W. Wiley Residence Hall
attributes.description: Previously known as the Men's Residence Hall H-3, the Harvey W. Wiley Residence Hall was built in 1958. The hall accommodated approximately 720 men and was financed by Housing and Home Finance Agency bonds and residence hall earnings.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Men's Residence Hall H-3 was renamed to Harvey W. Wiley Residence Hall in 1965. Wiley was a professor on campus and taught chemistry and physics.

attributes.Name: Newton Booth Tarkington Residence Hall
attributes.description: Tarkington Hall opened in 1958 and was originally called the Men's Residence Hall H-2. It is divided into four living units: Northeast, Southeast, Northwest, Southwest. The name was changed to Newton Booth Tarkington Residence Hall in 1965 in memory if Newton Booth Tarkington. This hall is now home to 708 male students as well as the Halberdier club and the Tarkington Market mini-mart.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building is named after Newton Booth Tarkington who was a generous contributor to Purdue University. Booth Tarkington attended Exeter Academy Prep School in New Hampshire, Purdue University, and Princeton University. He was a writer, playwright, artist, and world traveler. In 1919 and 1922 he received a Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.

attributes.Name: Dining Hall
attributes.description: Construction of the Oliver Perkins Terry house was completed in 1957. It was originally used for graduate students and Remington-Rand.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Mrs. Geraldine Terry (widow of the late Dr. O. P. Terry) desired to provide by donation a suitable memorial at or in connection with Purdue University to her late husband, Oliver Perkins Terry. The donation was $30,000. Part of this gift stipulated that the University must maintain an "Oliver Perkins Terry House."

attributes.Name: Purdue Village Apts #119
attributes.description: The first 58 Married Student Courts buildings were built in 1958. They were made of brick and steel and were built at a total cost of $10,200,000. They were built to replace the temporary barrack accommodations erected to house the influx of married students after World War II. Families were able to rent unfurnished two-bedroom apartments and single graduate students could rent furnished one or two-bedroom apartments. 16 more apartments were built in 1962 (Married Student Courts - II) and five apartments were added in 1967 (Married Student Courts - III). One of the original apartments was torn down in 2009 in order to make room for Discovery Park.

attributes.Name: Recreational Gymnasium
attributes.description: The recreational gymnasium was built in 1958. When it was built, it contained indoor and outdoor swimming pools, four basketball courts, space for badminton, volleyball, table tennis, rifle shooting, handball, squash, and other intramural activities. It also had administrative offices and men's and women's locker rooms.

attributes.Name: Equine Health Science Building
attributes.description: The Equine Health Science Building was originally known as the Bull Barn. It was built as part of a large construction project to create multiple buildings to be used for the school of Veterinary Science and Medicine. The total cost of constructing these buildings was $5,485,000. This building was originally used for the study of diseases pertaining to horse's feet and the reproductive problems of cattle. It was renamed the Farriery and then the Veterinary Farriery in 1963 and 1980 respectively. It was eventually renamed the Equine Health Sciences Building in 1999 and was later expanded.

attributes.Name: Veterinary Laboratory Animal Building
attributes.description: The Veterinary Laboratory Animal Building was built as part of a large construction project to create multiple buildings for the school of Veterinary Science and Medicine. The total cost of constructing these buildings was $5,485,000. This building was used for housing and production of laboratory animals.

attributes.Name: Veterinary Animal Isolation Building 2
attributes.description: The Veterinary Animal Isolation Building - 2 was built as part of a large construction project to create multiple buildings for the school of Veterinary Science and Medicine. The total cost of constructing these buildings was $5,485,000. This building was composed of 20 isolation rooms for research on infectious agents.

attributes.Name: Life Science Animal Building
attributes.description: Originally called the small animal building, the Life Science Animal Building was built with the Life Science Building (now the Lily Hall of Life Sciences), the Life Science Ranges and the Life Science Plant and Soils Laboratory. It originally housed the Departments of Biological Science, Animal Husbandry, Botany, and Plant Pathology and Agronomy.

attributes.Name: Center for Paralysis Research
attributes.description: The Center for Paralysis Research was previously known as the Veterinary Metabolic Disease Laboratory. It was built as part of a large construction project to create multiple buildings to be used for the school of Veterinary Science and Medicine. The total cost of constructing the Veterinary Medicine buildings was $5,485,000. This building was devoted to the study of physiological disorders and was renamed the Center for Paralysis Research in 1987.

attributes.Name: Basic Science Building and Animal Clinic
attributes.description: The Basic Science Building and Animal Clinic was completed 1960. It was built as part of a large construction project to create multiple buildings to be used for the school of Veterinary Science and Medicine. The total cost of constructing these buildings was $5,485,000. This building contained classroom-laboratories, research labs, a 4,000 square foot volume library, offices, preparation rooms, locker rooms, and service rooms.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Charles J. Lynn donated his Lynnwood Farm Property to Purdue University in July of 1942.  Included in his donation was the farming equipment, cattle, hogs, horses, and real estate on the property.

attributes.Name: Harriet O. and James M. Fowler Jr. Memorial House
attributes.description: The Harriet O. and James M. Fowler Jr. Memorial House was renovated and expanded in 1956. The expansion provided a dining hall service and recreational facilities for the State Street Court Residents. The old poultry building was rebuilt as the Poultry Science Building on the south side of State street immediately west of the Life Science Building.

attributes.Name: Purdue Memorial Union Club
attributes.description: The Purdue Memorial Union was added onto again in 1955. This addition provided 140 additional rooms for the Union Club Hotel and more than doubled the available rooms.

attributes.Name: Child Development and Family Studies Building
attributes.description: The Child Development and Family Studies Building was built in 1959. It was originally called the Family Life and Nursery No. 1., renamed the Child Development and Family Life Building, and renamed again to its current name in 1976. It was torn down in 2012.

attributes.Name: Heavilon Hall
attributes.description: The clock tower and front section of the old Heavilon Hall was removed in 1956 to make room for the new Heavilon Hall building. The clock and chimes from Heavilon Hall were stored to be used at a later date and were eventually placed in the new Bell Tower and Robert B. Gatewood wing of Mechanical Engineering.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building was named after Amos Heavilon, a farmer and businessman from Frankfort, who gave $35,000 to Purdue University in 1892. This money was applied to the erection costs of the Old Mechanical Engineering building.

attributes.Name: Agricultural Chemistry Building
attributes.description: A large addition was added to the Agricultural Chemistry Building in 1952. This addition provided the necessary space for testing of seeds, fertilizers and commercial feeds. The building started to house the Department of Biochemistry in 1953 and was renamed the Biochemistry Building in 1955.

attributes.Name: Smith Hall
attributes.description: Smith Hall was expanded in 1950. It added two large additions to the east and west sides of the north part of the building.

attributes.Name: Ray W. Herrick Laboratories
attributes.description: In 1959 an addition was added to the Horse Barn and it was renamed Herrick Laboratories. The new addition housed the research of refrigeration and air conditioning.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Named in honor of Ray W. Herrick who was "a pioneer in the air-conditioning industry and founder of Tecumseh Products.  Herrick supplied the money for Purdue students to tackle the industry issues of heating, ventilation, air-conditioning, and refrigeration."

attributes.Name: Greenhouses
attributes.description: The first three greenhouses of the Life Science ranges were constructed from 1951 to 1958.

attributes.Name: Dairy Barn
attributes.description: In 1951 the west wing of the Dairy Barn was removed to make room for the start of construction of the Lily Hall of Life Sciences.

attributes.Name: Faculty Housing
attributes.description: The Faculty Housing buildings were temporary houses that were built to meet the growing need of the university after World War II. Female enrollment largely increased between 1944-1945 leading to overcrowding at the university. After the war, many students were also now married and wanted to live with their families. This made the grouping of students into dormitories more difficult and increased the need for apartments at the university. These 23 homes were built at a total cost of approximately $29,000.

attributes.Name: Intramural Storage Shed
attributes.description: The Intramural Storage Shed is located northwest of the Northwest Chiller plan and next to the Intramural Playing Fields. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Food Stores Building
attributes.description: The Food Stores Building was built in 1960. It stored and directly delivered food and disposable items to Purdue's West Lafayette Campus.

attributes.Name: Hangar No. 4
attributes.description: Hangar No. 4 was constructed on Purdue's Airport to accommodate two DC6 aircraft used in the Midwest Program on Airborne Television Instruction (MPATI). This hangar was the base of operations for the MPATI. After MPATI, hangar #4 housed Purdue Aeronautics Corporations DC-6's and Purdue Airlines DC-9's.

attributes.Name: Utility Plant Storage Building
attributes.description: The Utility Plant Storage Building is located to the west of the Walter W. Wade Utility Plant.

attributes.Name: Wade Utility Plant Office Building
attributes.description: The Walter Utility Plant Office Building was located west of the Walter W. Wade Utility Plant. It was removed in 2000.

attributes.Name: Transportation Services Vehicle Storage
attributes.description: The Transportation Services Vehicle Storage buildings were built north of the experimental feed barn and food stores building. The buildings were torn down in 2015 to make room for the new Animal Sciences building. No other information is currently available regarding these buildings.

attributes.Name: Flight Operations Building
attributes.description: The Flight Operations Building was opened as a center for visiting pilots. It provided information, fuel sales, and transient registration.

attributes.Name: Tee-Hangar No. 1
attributes.description: The Tee-Hangar No. 1 is located slightly northwest of the Terminal building on the Purdue University Airport. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Life Science Ranges
attributes.description: Three greenhouses and a service building were added to the Lily Hall of Life Science in 1961. At this time, the greenhouses were renamed the Life Science Ranges.

attributes.Name: Grissom Hall
attributes.description: The Civil Engineering building was renovated in 1967 and renamed Grissom Hall in 1968.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Civil Engineering building was renamed Grissom Hall on May 2, 1968 after Virgil I. Grissom, the Lieutenant Colonial of the USAF. Virgil Grissom died January 27, 1967 alongside fellow astronauts Roger B. Chaffee and Edward H. White in a test-launch fire at Cape Canaveral, FL.

attributes.Name: Mechanical Engineering Building
attributes.description: An addition was added to the Mechanical Engineering building in 1950 and the Aeronautical Engineering Building was connected to the rest of the Mechanical Engineering Building. This addition made space for expansion of instruction and research.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Andrey A. Potter, Dean of Engineering, dedicated the Mechanical Engineering building to engineering education and research, stating that the betterment of society depended on the training and knowledge of engineers, and Purdue has a responsibility in producing well-rounded engineering graduates.

attributes.Name: Service Center
attributes.description: The Purdue shopping center was expanded in 1962. No other information is currently available regarding this addition.

attributes.Name: Holding Pen
attributes.description: Little is known about the construction of the Holding Pen. It was built during the same time period as the major construction of the rest of the Veterinary Complex in the early 1960s (Small and Large Animal Clinics, Lynn Hall, Metabolic Disease Lab, Farriery, Veterinary Laboratory Animal Building, Farriery).

attributes.Name: John T. McCutcheon Residence Hall
attributes.description: John T. McCutcheon Residence Hall was originally called the Men's Residence Hall H-4. It had eight stories and housed 748 students and 16 counselors. It was renamed John T. McCutcheon Residence Hall in 1965.
attributes.dedicationinfo:
McCutcheon Hall was named for John T. McCutcheon, an editorial cartoonist for the Chicago Tribune. John T. McCutcheon was born on May 6, 1870, in Tippecanoe County, the home of Purdue University. His grandparents emigrated from Scotland, thus the McCutcheon Hall club name of the "Royal Highlanders", after the Scottish clans, was adopted.

John T. McCutcheon graduated from Purdue in 1889. He worked at two Chicago newspapers, joining the Tribune in 1903. He retired from the Tribune in 1946. He was a world traveler and served as a war correspondent at the Battle of Manila Bay in 1898, the Boer War in South Africa, and World War I. He received the Pulitzer Prize for cartoons in 1931.

attributes.Name: Hangar No. 5
attributes.description: Hangar No. 5 was the 5th hangar built on the Purdue University Airport. It was "intended to be used for storage and minor maintenance of permanently-based and transient aircraft." It was also the fixed base operator.

attributes.Name: Civil Engineering Building
attributes.description: An addition was added to the Materials and Structural Testing Laboratories Building that was built in 1951. When the building was expanded it was renamed the Civil Engineering Building.

attributes.Name: Women's Residence Halls
attributes.description: The Women's Residence Halls Building was was constructed north of Meredith Hall. When it was built, it was the administration building for the women's residence halls.

attributes.Name: Grant Street Parking Garage
attributes.description: The original Grant Street Parking Garage was located on North Grant Street, across from the Purdue Memorial Union. When it was built it was a six-level garage that accommodated 627 cars. The garage contained a spiral ramp and was built for visitor parking. The building was torn down in 1994 and replaced with a new Grant Street Parking Garage in the same location.

attributes.Name: Benjamin Harrison Residence Hall
attributes.description: Benjamin Harrison Residence Hall was originally called Men's Residence H-5. It was built in the same style as the John T. McCutcheon Residence Hall that was built a few years before.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building was named after Benjamin Harrison who was the 23rd President of the United States. After his presidency, he returned to practicing law in Indianapolis and served on the Board of Trustees at Purdue University from July 1895 to March 1901. He was the most famous man to ever serve on the Board of Trustees and brought a plethora of experience in public life and world affairs.

attributes.Name: Guy J. Mackey Arena
attributes.description: The Purdue University Arena was built in 1967. It was located immediately north of Lambert Fieldhouse and was a brick-faced circular structure with a seating capacity for 14,416 people. It contained 6 main entrances and took just over 2 years to complete.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The arena was dedicated on December 2, 1967 during a ceremony that included the recognition of 10 former Boilermaker All-Americans. The ceremony was led by John Wooden and Charles "Stretch" Murphy. Indiana governor Roger Branigin also made a speech at the event. The building was dedicated to Guy J. Mackey in 1971 after his recent passing. Guy J. Mackey was the Athletic Director of Purdue University and was part of the Purdue Athletic program for 45 years.

attributes.Name: Well House No. 5
attributes.description: Well House No. 5 was built across the street from the Eleanor B. Shreve Residence Hall. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Track Toilet and Storage Building
attributes.description: The Track Toilet and Storage Building is located south of the Rankin Track and Field and North of the France A. Cordova Recreational Sports Building. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Entomology Environment Laboratory
attributes.description: A large addition was added to the Entomology Environment Laboratory in 1966.

attributes.Name: Mathematical Sciences Building
attributes.description: A 10 story structure that provides offices and classrooms for the mathematics department and mathematics extension, the administrative offices of the School of Science and the Computer Sciences Center.

attributes.Name: International Center Co-op House
attributes.description: Located at 525 Russell Street the International Center Co-op House was originally used as a Home Management practice house. These practice houses were used to allow students in the Home Economics department an opportunity to practice managing a home. This building went through multiple name and departmental changes but is currently used by the International Center. This building has 8 rooms that are used for long-term and short term rentals to Purdue students, as well as visiting students and faculty.

attributes.Name: George A. Hawkins Hall
attributes.description: Originally called Graduate House II, George A. Hawkins Hall consists of two wings. One wing is nine stories tall with double rooms and the other is 12-stories high with single rooms. It was built to accommodate 872 students and contains mechanical equipment on the top floor.  Several private baths are located on each floor and allow for rooms to be altered into suites if needed. It was renamed the Graduate House West in 1968 and then the George A. Hawkins Graduate House in 1981.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building is dedicated to George A. Hawkins who was an integral part in developing the engineering department at Purdue University. He was a student, faculty member, Dean of the School of Engineering, and Vice President for Academic Affairs at the university for many years. He also was a leading researcher in the field of heat transfer.

attributes.Name: Tee-Hangar No. 2
attributes.description: Tee-Hangar No. 2 was built with Tee-Hangar No. 3 on the Purdue University Airport. The two hangars were built together at a total cost of $45,081. Tee-Hangar No. 2 was used for aircraft storage.

attributes.Name: Tee-Hangar No. 3
attributes.description: Tee-Hangar No. 3 was built with Tee-Hangar No. 2 on the Purdue University Airport. Both buildings were built together at a total cost of $45,081. Tee-Hangar No. 3 was used for aircraft storage.

attributes.Name: Physics Building
attributes.description: An addition to  the Physics Building was completed in 1970.
attributes.dedicationinfo: On January 20th, 1970, the Physics Building Accelerator Facility was named the Karl Lark-Horovitz Laboratory of Nuclear Structure in honor of Dr. Karl Lark-Horovitz. Horovitz was an outstanding faculty member at Purdue University.

attributes.Name: Robert E. Heine Pharmacy Building
attributes.description: The Robert E. Heine Pharmacy Building is a six-story structure that provided offices, classrooms, a library, and animal research facilities for the School of Pharmacy and Pharmacal Sciences. The Naval Armory Building was demolished to make room for this new building. It was originally called the Pharmacy Building and was renamed the Robert E. Heine Pharmacy Building in 1985.
attributes.dedicationinfo: In 1985 the Pharmacy Building was named after Robert E. Heine. Mr. Heine was a Purdue alumni, trustee, and benefactor.

attributes.Name: Oliver Perkins Terry House
attributes.description: An addition to the Oliver Perkins Terry house was completed in 1965.

attributes.Name: Service Building & Greenhouse
attributes.description: Two more greenhouse units were added to the Horticulture Greenhouse. The addition was built for the study of pesticides. In 1977, the name was changed back to the Horticultural Greenhouse.

attributes.Name: Eleanor B. Shreve Residence Hall
attributes.description: The Eleanor B. Shreve Residence Hall was originally called Women's Residence Hall H-9. The residence hall contains 890 beds and was renamed the Eleanor B. Shreve Residence Hall in 1967. When it was built, it was the largest co-ed residence hall on campus and contained lounges, activity spaces, and residences support centers.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Shreve Residence Hall was named after Eleanor Burns Shreve who was a writer, activist, and musician.

attributes.Name: International Center Office/Classroom Building
attributes.description: Located at 523 Russell Street, the International Center Office/Classroom Building was originally used as a Home Management practice house. These practice houses were used to allow students in the Home Economics department an opportunity to practice managing a home. This building went through multiple name and departmental changes but is currently used by the International Center. This center offers meeting room and kitchen facility rentals to organizations, business groups, and individuals.

attributes.Name: Well House No. 6
attributes.description: Well House No. 6 was built next to the Northwest Chiller Plant. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Golf Course Maintenance Barn
attributes.description: The Golf Course Maintenance Barn stands on the Birck Boilermaker Golf Complex near where the Ollman Golfcart Barn stands today. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Black Cultural Center
attributes.description: The original Black Cultural Center was a two-story cinder block and wood house across the street from the Armory. It also had an attic and a basement. The Black Cultural Center was relocated to a new building in 1998.

attributes.Name: Golf Storage Maintenance Barn
attributes.description: The Golf Storage Maintenance Barn stands on the Birck Boilermaker Golf Complex near where the Ollman Golfcart Barn stands today. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Smith Hall
attributes.description: An addition and renovation to Smith Hall was completed in 1977. This renovation occurred in two phases. The first phase began in 1971 and the second phase began in 1974.

attributes.Name: Northwestern Avenue - Parking Garage
attributes.description: A parking garage was built between Northwestern and Grant Street in 1975.

attributes.Name: Well House No. 7
attributes.description: Well House No. 7 was built across the street from the Hillenbrand Residence Hall. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Ray W. Herrick Laboratories
attributes.description: An addition was added to the previously built Herrick Laboratories in 1974. The expansion was slightly more than 2,000 square feet of semi-anechoic laboratory, that was used for noise and vibration studies of transportation vehicles and other machinery. It included an instrument room and space to house dynamometers and motors.

attributes.Name: Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory
attributes.description: The Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory was built in 1949 to provide and confirm field diagnoses of disease conditions in animals. When it was built, it was connected to the Postmortem Laboratory. It was renamed the Veterinary Animal Diagnostic Laboratory in 1968.

attributes.Name: Marstellar Street Parking Garage
attributes.description: The Marstellar Street Parking Garage was built between Sheetz and Marstellar Street in 1976. The garage provided space for about 525 cars. Ongoing maintenance costs were cited as cause for its demolition in 2016.

attributes.Name: A. A. Potter Engineering Center
attributes.description: In 1974, work began on the four-story A. A. Potter Engineering Center. The building was built to house the Institute of Interdisciplinary Engineering Studies and contained research centers, laboratories, and a library. The building was funded by the 1969 Centennial Fund Campaign and Lilly Endowment fund.
attributes.dedicationinfo: In April, 1977, the building was dedicated in honor of Andrey A. Potter. Potter was the dean of Engineering at Purdue from 1920 to 1953. He also developed steam turbines, was a professor of mechanical engineering, and helped to improve the Purdue College of Engineering. From 1945-1946 he also served as the interim president of Purdue University.

attributes.Name: Grounds Service Building
attributes.description: Two large sheds were added to the back of the old Livestock Judging Pavilion. No other information is currently available regarding this addition.

attributes.Name: Horticultural Greenhouse
attributes.description: Units 9 and 10 were removed and Unit 8 was expanded in the Horticulture Greenhouse.

attributes.Name: Hangar No. 6
attributes.description: Hangar No. 6 was built on the Purdue University airport in 1967.

attributes.Name: International Center
attributes.description: The International Center was located on Marsteller Street until it was moved to 523 and 525 Russell Street in 1998. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Psychological Sciences Building
attributes.description: The Psychological Sciences Building was constructed from 1978 to 1983 and was connected to the north end of Peirce Hall.

attributes.Name: Composites Laboratory
attributes.description: This Composites Laboratory is located south of the Aerospace Science Laboratory and is used for research in composite materials and structures. In 1993, the name of the lab was changed to McDonnell Douglas Composite Materials Laboratory in appreciation of a gift fund from the McDonnell Douglas Foundation.

attributes.Name: Airport Service Building
attributes.description: The Airport Service Building was "used for storage of grounds service vehicles and sand necessary to maintain the airport runways during periods of snow and ice." It also housed grass cutting equipment and an office restroom. This equipment was previously stored in a large hanger that was re-purposed to be used by Air Wisconsin.

attributes.Name: Soil Erosion Lab
attributes.description: The Soil Erosion Lab is USDA-owned and sits on Purdue's land through a land lease with the federal government. It is a one-story building, containing about 35,000 square feet of space that is used for the study of soil erosion patterns and the infiltration of fertilizers into water supplies. The building contains a variety of research equipment, including a mechanism that can simulate the effect of ran on soil.

attributes.Name: Wood Street Parking Garage
attributes.description: The Wood Street Parking Garage was built on the corner of Grant and Wood Street and contained spaces for 1,000 cars. It was the 5th parking garage built on campus.

attributes.Name: John C. Smalley Center for Housing & Food Service Administration
attributes.description: An addition was added to the Women's Residence Administration Building in 1982. It was renamed the John C. Smalley Center for Housing and Food Services Administration in 1985.
attributes.dedicationinfo: John C. Smalley was born in West Lafayette and graduated from Purdue. He worked for Purdue's Residence Halls System for thirty-seven years and dedicated his time to the Memorial Union. He also became the University's first Vice President for Housing and Food Services in 1975.

attributes.Name: Veterinary Laboratory Animal Storage Building
attributes.description: The Veterinary Laboratory Animal Storage Building was built at the south end of the Veterinary Science pasture in 1980.

attributes.Name: Agricultural Engineering Machine Storage Building
attributes.description: The Agricultural Engineering Machine Storage Building was built on the northern end of the Purdue University Airport.  It appeared to have been moved or rebuilt in 1995 to the west of this location. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Golf Cart Maintenance Buildings
attributes.description: The Golf Cart Maintenance Buildings were located by the Melvin L. Ollman Golf Cart Barn and Pete Dye Clubhouse on the Purdue Golf Course. The buildings were removed in 2015. No other information is currently available regarding these structures.

attributes.Name: Maurice G. Knoy Hall of Technology
attributes.description: Originally called the Technology Building, the Maurice G. Know Hall of Technology was built in 1985. It was the first building on Purdue's campus to use solar power and has photovoltaic arrays on its roof. It also contains the BoilerMAKER lab which is a place where students can use 3D printers to make their virtual designs come to life.

attributes.Name: Building Services and Grounds Building
attributes.description: The Building Services and Grounds Building was originally called Mechanical Systems Operations Building and then Facilities Service Building. The building was torn down in 2015 to make room for Hobart and Russell Creighton Hall of Animal Sciences and Land O'Lakes Center for Experiential Learning & the Purina Pavilion.

attributes.Name: Veterinary Pathobiology Research Laboratory
attributes.description: An addition was added to the Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory and Postmortem Laboratory in 1978. When the addition was built, the two buildings were still referred to as two separate entities. Both buildings began being referred to as one building (the Veterinary Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory) in 1981.

attributes.Name: Northwestern Avenue Parking Garage
attributes.description: An addition was added to the original Northwestern Avenue Parking Garage in 1986 and the building was renamed the Northwestern Avenue Parking Garage. This added spaces for 700-1,000 cars and a visitors center  "which would house parking activities for staff an visitors." This was the 6th parking garage built on campus.

attributes.Name: Visitor Information Center
attributes.description: Originally called the Visitor Information Center, the Purdue Graduate Student Center is located in the Northwestern Avenue Parking Garage. When it was built, it housed the parking activities for staff and visitors. In January 2013, the visitor center moved to room 110 in the Purdue Memorial Union so that they could be right "at the front door" of Purdue for all of the campuses visitors. This portion of the Northwestern Avenue Parking Garage now houses the Purdue Graduate Student Center. This center is home to the Purdue Graduate Student Government, the Black Graduate Student Association, and  has office space for graduate student legal services.

attributes.Name: Utility Plant Office Building
attributes.description: The Utility Plant Office Building is a small building that is attached to southeast end of the the Walter W. Wade Utility Plant.

attributes.Name: Laboratory Materials Storage Building
attributes.description: The Laboratory Materials Storage Building is a centralized facility where waste and/or surplus laboratory materials generated by the University's many research laboratories can be analyzed, segregated, stored, and prepared for reuse or disposal. It contains offices, analytical laboratories, space for storage of chemicals and waste materials, and space for blending, neutralizing and recycling.

attributes.Name: Bridge between PHYS & MSEE
attributes.description: A skybridge connects the Physics Building (PHYS) and Materials and Electrical Engineering (MSEE) building together.

attributes.Name: Bridge between MSEE & EE
attributes.description: A skybridge connects the Materials and Electrical Engineering (MSEE) building and Electrical Engineering (EE) building together.

attributes.Name: Civil Engineering Building
attributes.description: The first phase of an addition to the Civil Engineering building began in 1986. It was built as part of the expansion of the Engineering and Geosciences Facilities. It created laboratories for Geomatic Engineering and Geotechnical Engineering.

attributes.Name: Materials and Electrical Engineering
attributes.description: Originally called the Engineering and Geoscience Complex, the Materials and Electrical Engineering Building (MSEE) was built in 1988. It contains an open two-story glassed atrium, two laboratory facilities, and two pedestrian skyways that connect this building to the Electrical Engineering and Physics building. The two laboratories in the building are the Turner Laboratory which is used by Electrical Engineering and Materials Engineering and the Integrated Optics Laboratory which has a "clean room" that is used to grow new materials atom by atom.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The dedication of this building was part of a three-day Centennial Celebration for the School of Electrical Engineering.

attributes.Name: Women's Golf Locker Room
attributes.description: The Women's Golf Locker Room was built on the Purdue Golf Course on Cherry Lane. The locker was built in order to replace the outdated facilities that were too small and did not have enough showers.

attributes.Name: Delon and Elizabeth Hampton Hall of Civil Engineering
attributes.description: Phase II of an addition to the Civil Engineering Building was completed in 1990.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Hampton Hall was named for Delon Hamptom and his mother Elizabeth Hamptom. Delon Hampton made a $7.5 million donation to the School of Civil Engineering, earned a masters degree from Purdue in 1958, a doctorate in civil engineering in 1961, and an honorary degree from Purdue in 1994. The ceremony for the Delon and Elizabeth Hampton Hall of Civil Engineering was held on September 14, 2012 in Stadium Mall. The ceremony lasted from 3pm to 4pm.

attributes.Name: Lytle J. Freehafer Hall of Administration Services
attributes.description: Lytle J. Freehafer Hall of Administration had a three-story, 28,000 gross square foot addition added in 1988. It was similar to the previously existing open landscape offices and had several enclosed conference rooms.

attributes.Name: Mollenkopf Athletic Center
attributes.description: Originally called the Indoor Practice Facility, the Mollenkopf Athletic Center was built in 1990. When the Athletic center was built, it contained a full indoor practice field and a two-story weight room. The third floor and mezzanine were completed in 1994 and the AstroTurf was replaced with FieldTurf in 2006 and 2017.

attributes.Name: Walter W. Wade Utility Plant
attributes.description: The Walter W. Wade Utility Plant was expanded in 1989 to further take over the function of the old North Power Plant. It included the addition of a boiler and water chiller.

attributes.Name: University Street Parking Garage
attributes.description: An addition was added to the University Street Parking Garage in 1989. It provided spaces for 754 cars and was the seventh parking garage built on campus.

attributes.Name: Class of 1950 Lecture Hall
attributes.description: The Class of 1950 Lecture Hall was constructed in place of the old physics building. It consists of an auditorium which seats 500 and three additional classrooms which can accommodate 29-40 people each. The main lecture auditorium consists of modern audiovisual technology and state-of-the-art acoustics to allow for a better learning environment. The building is made up of brick and is supported on the first level by large brick columns, with the second floor wall being made of windows. Inside the southwest column is a time capsule of the Class of 1950. On the second floor there is a 700 pound bronze statue of two classmates from the Class of 1950 entitled "The Way It Was." The Class of 1950 Lecture Hall is located on Oval Drive next to Stanley Coulter Hall and is connected to Peirce Hall and the Psychological Sciences building.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The cornerstone was laid during Gala week of 1990, the formal dedication ceremony took place during homecoming 1990, on October 20th. The building is dedicated to the class of 1950 due to their very generous gift of over $1 million.

attributes.Name: Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory
attributes.description: The new Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (ADDL)  was constructed just south of the original Animal Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (currently the Veterinary Pathobiology Research Laboratory) and the Animal Isolation Units. It serves Indiana in diagnosing animal diseases, providing assistance in maintaining animal health and well-being, and ensuring nutritious and disease-free food products. It is a three-story building which has laboratory spaces for serology, histology, virology, pathology, microbiology, toxicology, and avian specimens, an electron microscopy room, an avian necropsy room, a specimen prep room, a postmortem floor, and an incinerator. It also has several locker rooms and viewing rooms for students.

attributes.Name: Food Stores Building
attributes.description: An addition was added to the Food Stores Building in 1991. It added freezer, cooler, processing, humidity control, and dry storage areas.

attributes.Name: Animal Science Teaching Laboratory
attributes.description: Originally named the Animal Pavilion, the Animal Sciences Teaching Laboratory was renamed in 1991. The building was used for instruction in Animal Science and was torn down in 2018.

attributes.Name: McCutcheon Drive Parking Garage
attributes.description: The McCutcheon Drive Parking Garage was built in 1990.

attributes.Name: Hillenbrand Residence Hall
attributes.description: The Hillenbrand Residence Hall was built in 1994 and provided housing for 800 students.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Hillenbrand Residence Hall was named for a father and son who each served as a member of the Board of Trustees. John Hillenbrand served on Purdue's Board of Trustees from 1913 to 1947. His 34 years of service as a trustee is the longest in University history. His son, William A. Hillenbrand, was appointed to the Board of Trustees in 1967. He served as a member until 1975. John and William Hillenbrand were both lifelong residents of Batesville, Indiana, where they ran a family business and participated in numerous community activities.

attributes.Name: Laboratory Material Storage Trailer
attributes.description: The Laboratory Materials Storage Trailer is located southeast of the Hazardous Materials Management Trailer. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Materials Management & Distribution Center
attributes.description: The Materials Management & Distribution Center provides facilities for General Stores, Central Receiving, and Campus Mail Service. It was originally called the Warehouse Building and was renamed the Materials Management and Distribution Center.

attributes.Name: Grounds Service Salt Storage
attributes.description: The Grounds Service Salt Storage building was used for salt storage. It was torn down in 2011 to make room for the Martin C. Jischke Hall of Biomedical Engineering. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Grounds Training Conference Room
attributes.description: The Grounds Training Conference Room was used for grounds training. It was torn down in 2004 to make room for Herrick Laboratories and the Martin C. Jischke Hall of Biomedical Engineering. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Animal Holding Facility
attributes.description: Phase I of construction of the Animal Holding Facility was completed in 1991. When it was built, this building housed 60 dogs and included a treatment room, diet preparation and food storage areas, receiving quarantine and isolation rooms, and a mangers office.

attributes.Name: Materials Management Storage Building 1
attributes.description: The Materials Management Storage Building 1 is located west of the Materials Management Distribution Center on the southern edge of campus.

attributes.Name: Purdue Bell Tower
attributes.description: The Purdue Bell Tower is approximately 160 feet tall and is located south of the Elliott Hall of Music. The bell and clock tower incorporated design elements and the bells of the old Heavilon Hall tower that was removed in 1956. The bell tower was sponsored by the Class of 1948.

attributes.Name: Grant Street Parking Garage
attributes.description: The current Grant Street Parking Garage was constructed in 1995. It was built in place of the old Grant Street Parking Garage that opened in 1965 and was torn down in 1994. The parking garage provided 1,450 parking spaces.

attributes.Name: Walter W. Wade Utility Plant
attributes.description: The Walter W. Wade Utility Plant was expanded again in 1997. The expansion included the addition of a cooling tower, turbine generator, and coal handling system.

attributes.Name: Charles J. Lynn Hall of Veterinary Medicine
attributes.description: An addition was added to the Basic Science Building and Animal Clinic and Large Animal Clinic in 1996.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building was dedicated to Charles J. Lynn.

attributes.Name: Telecommunications Building
attributes.description: The Telecommunications Building was built and then the new phone lines were added on campus. According to the Financial Report, the "Telecommunications Project" was built for a total cost of $40,000,000.

attributes.Name: Physical Facilities Service Building
attributes.description: Construction of the Physical Facilities Service Building was completed in 1998.

attributes.Name: Oliver Perkins Terry Garage
attributes.description: A small two car garage was built in 1996 and is attached to the Oliver Perkins Terry House. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Purdue West - Building B
attributes.description: The two shopping and service centers were combined in 1996. It is now home to the Center for Healthy Living, Follett's Purdue West Bookstore, and a Dairy Queen.

attributes.Name: Agricultural Engineering Machine Storage Building
attributes.description: The Agricultural Engineering Machine Storage Building appeared to be rebuilt or moved in 1995. The building was removed in 2009 and a new ADM Agricultural Innovation Center was built by the new grounds and maintenance facilities south of campus.

attributes.Name: Veterinary Laboratory Animal Storage Building
attributes.description: The Veterinary Laboratory Animal Storage Building was expanded in 1996. No other information is currently available regarding this addition.

attributes.Name: Philip E. Nelson Hall of Food Science
attributes.description: Originally called the Food Science Building, the Philip E. Nelson Hall of Food Science is a 60,000 square foot laboratory, classroom, and office facility. The building contains eighty offices, five classrooms and teaching laboratories, and thirty eight research laboratories. It was renamed the Philip E. Nelson Hall of Food Science in 2010.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Food Science Building was named in honor of Philip E. Nelson, who developed the Food Science program into one of the strongest in the nation. He also became an international laureate for his work in improving the world's food supply.

attributes.Name: Coating Application Research Laboratory
attributes.description: Located near the Purdue University airport, the Coating Application Research Laboratory is used for research in coating application. It contains industrial production lines, application booths, drying mechanisms, and temperature and humidity controls that can be used to mimic various climates.

attributes.Name: Stanley Coulter
attributes.description: A three story addition was added to the north end of the Biology Building in 1994.

attributes.Name: Samuel Voinoff Golf Pavilion
attributes.description: The Samuel Voinoff Golf Pavilion was built as part of the remodeling of the Kampen Golf Course. The cost of constructing the entire north course was $8.5 million and includes remodeling the golf course and building the Pete Dye Clubhouse, Melvin Ollman Golf Cart Barn, and the Samuel Voinoff Golf Pavilion.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The golf shelter was "named for the late Samuel Voinoff, (a) Purdue golf coach from 1950 to 1974 and a Purdue alumnus."

attributes.Name: Pete Dye Clubhouse
attributes.description: The Pete Dye Clubhouse was part of the remodeling of the Kampen Golf Course. The cost of constructing the entire north course was $8.5 million and includes remodeling the golf course and building the Pete Dye Clubhouse, Melvin Ollman Golf Cart Barn, and the Samuel Voinoff Golf Pavilion.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The clubhouse was dedicated to Pete Dye who redesigned the Birck Boilermaker Golf Complex. "Dye, who took classes at Purdue during the 1950s, was named the 'architect of the year' by Golf World magazine. He designed a number of public and private courses, including several in Indiana."

attributes.Name: Black Cultural Center
attributes.description: The Black Cultural Center is a building that is made of brick, concrete, and stone. The building contains multiple architectural features that mirror traditional African designs.The building also contains a multipurpose room, lounge, computer lab, and library.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Black Cultural Center was dedicated on homecoming weekend, October 15-16, 1999. Trustee Powers described seeing the return of black alumni to the dedication of the new Black Cultural Center was "a truly touching experience."

attributes.Name: Utility Plant Office Building
attributes.description: The Utility Plant Office Building was built northwest of the Wade Utility Plant.

attributes.Name: Purdue Pride Store
attributes.description: The Purdue Pride Store is connected to the Northern end of Ross-Ade Stadium. It is now called the Purdue Team Store.

attributes.Name: Northwest Chiller Plant
attributes.description: The Northwest Chiller Plant was added onto in 2012. During this addition, a 2700-ton chiller was added. The new chiller helped to meet the need for chilled water cooling due to campus expansion.

attributes.Name: Ross-Ade Stadium
attributes.description: From 2001-2003 Ross-Ade Stadium underwent a major renovation. It was said to have made the stadium the "most attractive and fan-friendly stadium in all of college football". This renovation occurred in three phases. Phase I included structural and concrete repairs, expanded restrooms and concession facilities, wider aisles in the concourse for people movement, private viewing suites, and club seating on the west side of the stadium. Phase II included the addition of an upper deck on the east side, additional restrooms and concession facilities, and a connecting bridge on the west main concourse that was constructed around the south end of the stadium. Phase III completed the plan with the addition of an upper deck on the north end.

attributes.Name: David C. Pfendler Hall of Agriculture
attributes.description: The David C. Pfendler Hall of Agriculture had a major addition added from 2001-2004. The renovation included the addition of 25,000 square feet of classroom and laboratory space. The renovation also addressed safety hazards that caused the university to stop scheduling classes in Pfendler hall in 1999.

attributes.Name: Forney Hall of Chemical Engineering
attributes.description: An addition was added to the Chemical Engineering Building from 2002-2004. The project name was "Chemical Engineering Addition - 2002." The addition includes a new 200-seat auditorium and two 60-seat classrooms, as well as a hands-on laboratory, advanced student research laboratory, and new labs for bio-engineering, catalysis, and nanoscience research. It is equipped with state-of-the-art research technology and high-performance instruments.

attributes.Name: Physical Facilities Service Building
attributes.description: An addition was added to the Physical Facilities Service Building in 2002.

attributes.Name: Bridge between KRAN & RAWL
attributes.description: A skybridge connects the Krannert Graduate School of Management (KRAN) and Jerry S. Rawls Hall (RAWL) together. The skybridge stretches over Grant Street.

attributes.Name: Life Science Ranges
attributes.description: An additional set of greenhouses were added to the Life Sciences Plant and Soils Laboratory in 2003. No other information is currently available regarding this addition.

attributes.Name: Bindley Bioscience Center
attributes.description: The Bindley Bioscience Center was completed in 2006.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Bindley Bioscience Center is named for the 1962 Purdue graduate, William E. Bindley, who, in 2002, contributed $52.5 million to the university. Bindley designated $7.5 million of his gift to cover half the cost of the two-story, 50,000-square-foot research facility, with the rest funded by earnings from unrestricted endowments. The center opened to researchers in October 2005.

attributes.Name: Veterinary Medicine Isolation Facility
attributes.description: The Veterinary Medicine Isolation Facility was originally known as the Large Animal Isolation Unit. It is an eight-stall building that is completely separate from the Veterinary Teaching Hospital. It is mainly used for treating horses but one stall is used for cattle. The separation of this building from the main hospital helps to insure that an infectious animal cannot contaminate non-infected hospital patients. The building also contains a treatment room, a sterilization room, two small storage rooms, and office space. A large mechanical room is the largest room in the building and houses specialized air-handling equipment.

attributes.Name: Purdue Exponent Building
attributes.description: Located on Northwestern Avenue, the Purdue Exponent Building was home to the Purdue Exponent. In 2017, the Exponent moved it's press equipment to a larger facility at North Ninth Street and Widewater Drive in Lafayette. The newsroom and business office remained on the second floor at the the Northwestern Avenue location and the University Lutheran Church purchased the remainder of the building. The Lutheran Church opened a worship sanctuary on the third floor of the building and the basement, that previously housed the press equipment, was converted into a gym/fellowship hall. The first floor will also be occupied by the Lutheran Church and will contain offices and a cafe.

attributes.Name: Utility Plant Office Facility
attributes.description: The Utility Plant Office Facility was built in 2004 and is located north of the Walter Wade Utility Plant.

attributes.Name: Equine Health Sciences Annex
attributes.description: The Equine Health Sciences Annex was built at the southern end of the Veterinary Medicine Complex. The Annex offers both housing and ample room to carry out procedures for research and teaching purposes. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Mechanical Engineering Building
attributes.description: The Robert B. Gatewood Wing was added to the Mechanical Engineering Building in 2009. The Roger B. Gatewood Wing was the first Purdue building constructed to environmental standards set by the U.S. Green Building Council. It added approximately 41,000 square feet to the Mechanical Engineering Building and increased its space by 55 percent. The centerpiece of the Gatewood Wing is the Dr. Milton B. Hollander Atrium, which spotlights mechanical engineering as Purdue's first engineering discipline. The clock from the original Heavilon Hall (the first mechanical engineering building) was placed in the atrium and is used as a working model with all of its components clearly visible. The space also showcases student projects and serves as a venue for student design competitions and recruiting events.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The wing of the Mechanical Engineering Building was named after Roger B. Gatewood. Gatewood, a 1968 graduate, gave the key leadership gift to the School of Mechanical Engineering in 2003 to support the new learning and research facility. Purdue University celebrated the successful completion of fundraising for the $33 million state-of- the-art Gatewood Wing on Thursday October 25th, 2007.

attributes.Name: Fuel Oil Tank
attributes.description: The fuel oil tank was built south of campus and sits next to the waste water retention tank and laboratory materials storage building. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Water Cooling Vent Tower A
attributes.description: The Water Cooling Vent Towers are 6 cooling vents located south of the Walter Wade Utility Plant. No other information is currently available regarding these structures.

attributes.Name: Water Cooling Vent Tower B
attributes.description: The Water Cooling Vent Towers are 6 cooling vents located south of the Walter Wade Utility Plant. No other information is currently available regarding these structures.

attributes.Name: Water Cooling Vent Tower C
attributes.description: The Water Cooling Vent Towers are 6 cooling vents located south of the Walter Wade Utility Plant. No other information is currently available regarding these structures.

attributes.Name: Water Cooling Vent Tower E
attributes.description: The Water Cooling Vent Towers are 6 cooling vents located south of the Walter Wade Utility Plant. No other information is currently available regarding these structures.

attributes.Name: Water Cooling Vent Tower F
attributes.description: The Water Cooling Vent Towers are 6 cooling vents located south of the Walter Wade Utility Plant. No other information is currently available regarding these structures.

attributes.Name: Water Cooling Vent Tower D
attributes.description: The Water Cooling Vent Towers are 6 cooling vents located south of the Walter Wade Utility Plant. No other information is currently available regarding these structures.

attributes.Name: Neil Armstrong Hall of Engineering
attributes.description: Ground broke for the Neil Armstrong Hall of Engineering in 2004. The building contains classrooms and laboratories that are intended to encourage teamwork and exploration in the field of engineering. The building houses the School of  Aeronautics and Astronautics, the School of Materials Engineering, and the School of Engineering Education. It also contains an offices for the Dean of Engineering, the Engineering Projects in Community Service (EPICS), as well as the Minority Engineering Program and Women in Engineering Program. In front of the building is a bronze statue that depicts Neil Armstrong as an undergraduate student.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building is dedicated to Neil Armstrong. Neil Armstrong graduated from Purdue's School of Aeronautics and Astronautics in 1955 with his bachelor's degree. He was selected for astronaut training in 1962 and, in 1969, was the first person to walk on the moon during NASA's Apollo 11 mission. He was also a combat pilot during the Korean war, the spacecraft commander for the Gemini 8 flight in 1966, and a test pilot. Following his NASA career, Armstrong frequently visited Purdue and took part in university initiatives. The building was funded by state funds and private donations.

attributes.Name: McCutcheon Street Parking Garage
attributes.description: An addition to the McCutcheon Parking Garage was added in 1990. This addition was built to replace the lost parking that was removed to make room for the construction of a new residence hall west of Fowler Hall. This parking garage included 1,060 parking spaces.

attributes.Name: Gerald D. and Edna E. Mann Hall
attributes.description: Originally called the e-Enterprise Center, the Gerald D. and Edna E. Mann Hall was built in 2007. It is a two-story structure that contains space for 100 researchers and staff in the areas of health-care engineering, advanced manufacturing, cancer care, homeland security.
attributes.dedicationinfo: A dedication ceremony took place at Mann Hall, 203 S. Intramural Drive, on the southwest edge of campus. Gerald "Jerry" Mann and his wife, Edna, donated the initial $3 million for constructing the building. The Lilly Endowment gave $2 million to create two endowed positions: a directorship for the e-Enterprise Center, and the Gerald and Edna Mann director of the Bindley Bioscience Center. The balance went to the building fund.

attributes.Name: Latino Cultural Center
attributes.description: The Latino Cultural Center was located at 600 N. Russell Street and was a center for Hispanic and Latin Culture. It was a place where student could go for support, mentorship, and friendship. It provided programs ranging from lectures and entertainment and it was open to all Purdue students, faculty and staff. In 2017, the Latino Cultural Center was moved to 426 Waldron Street and the old center was planned to be replaced with a parking lot.

attributes.Name: Printing Services Facility
attributes.description: The Printing Services department was relocated from Harrison St. and Martin Jischke Dr. to a new facility located south of campus. The building was designed to house multiple offices and space for large-scale printing presses, high-volume digital copiers, mail production, and paper storage.

attributes.Name: Windsor Dining Court
attributes.description: A major addition was added to the Windsor Hall complex in 2005. The addition was part of a major project to consolidate all dining courts on campus. The American School and University magazine selected this dining court and profiled it in its August 2008 Education Interiors Showcase issue.The dining court also won a third national outstanding design award.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The private dining room in the Windsor Dining Court was dedicated on Friday November 21st. This room was dedicated in honor of Betty Arnsman, who served Purdue Housing and Food Services for more than 30 years. She helped to consolidate the men and women's residential system in 1969 and helped to create one of he nations largest on-campus housing programs. As stated in a Purdue News article "'Betty dedicated her career to education and the personal development, growth and life-planning of students, particularly for women,' Sautter said.'She brought to her profession and her daily life the highest standards of ethics, integrity and honesty and was an exceptional role model for students and colleagues.'"

attributes.Name: Animal Holding Facility
attributes.description: Phase III of the construction of the Animal Holding Facility was completed in 2001. The addition added space for 72 dogs and offices for the university veterinary staff.

attributes.Name: Wiley Dining Court
attributes.description: The Wiley Dining Court is located immediately south of Wiley Hall. It is a freestanding dining court that holds 500 seats and was part of the project to consolidate the 11 dining rooms on campus into five distinct dining courts.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Wiley Dining court was dedicated on October 2, 2008. Many people were in attendance including France A. Córdova, Karie Glebe the Dining court manager, and Sarah Johnson the director of dining services. The Wiley Hall general manager cut the ribbon at the ceremony.

attributes.Name: Pharmacy Building
attributes.description: Originally called the Laboratory, the Pharmacy building was completed in 1874 and was constructed using brick. It was two stories tall with a one-story extension and a high basement. It contained about twenty rooms and originally housed the school of pharmacy, the department of chemistry, the department of physics, the department of mechanics, and the department of civil engineering. The main portion of the structure contained a lecture room, balance room, store rooms, office, reading room, pharmacognosy room, prescription room, and special laboratories. The general laboratory occupied the extension, and furnished accommodations for 130 students. In 1881, an addition was added to make additional room for the School of Mechanics. The building was expanded in 1889 so that the School of Pharmacy had its own separate laboratory at the rear of the building. In 1893, the building was renamed the Pharmacy Building and it was renamed Building No. 2 in 1932.The building was eventually demoli...

attributes.Name: Locomotive Museum 1
attributes.description: In 1902 the first Locomotive Museum was built under the recommendation of Dean Goss. Goss wanted to preserve interesting locomotives in order to educate engineers of the future. The Locomotive Museum was an inexpensive shed that was build over the Locomotive exhibit. The collection included the "Tornado" (the second locomotive used on the Seaboard Air Line, built in 1840, donated to Purdue in 1902), an old coach used on the Boston Providence Railroad in 1835 that was drawn by horses, Winan' Camel Back (built by Baltimore and Ohio in 1868, given to Purdue in 1901), Chicago and Northwestern Locomotive (built in 1873 and given to Purdue in 1905), Daniel Nason engine (built in 1858, part of the equipment of the old Boston and Providence, and given to Purdue in 1905), the Eddy or "Mamosa" locomotive (built by Boston and Albany in 1876, given to Purdue in 1908), the Reuben Wells locomotive (built in 1858), an old railway track (the oldest track in the exhibit is from Baltimore and Ohio Ra...

attributes.Name: Armory
attributes.description: In 1908, the original Military Hall/Armory was moved to where the front entrance of the Armory stands today. This move created space for the new gymnasium (Felix Haas Hall). In the early in the morning of February 24, 1916, the Armory was destroyed by a fire. The Board of Trustees minutes of March 28, 1916 states, "The fire was discovered at 3:50 a.m. in a small room at the north end of the building and was under such headway that within a few moments the entire upper part of the building burst into flames. It was impossible under any circumstances to save the building or its contents. In the room where the fire was discovered was a small coal stove in which the fire had been banked by the janitor for the night. In the absence of any definite information as to the cause of the fire, it can only be assumed that it resulted from this stove. There is no evidence of neglect on the part of any one having the care of the building. The night watchman passed the building at 3:30 a.m. but co...

attributes.Name: Franklin Levering Cary Quadrangle (East)
attributes.description: The Franklin Levering Cary Quadrangle (East) building is the first of the Franklin Levering Cary Quadrangle buildings. The cornerstone was laid on November 5, 1927. When it was built, it was a 42 x 269 foot structure that was made of of brick, stone, and reinforced concrete. It was three stories high with a basement and contained quarters for 153 male students, a manager's suite, a large dining room, a completely equipped kitchen, three lounges, and a heating plant of its own. It was designed with Tudor Gothic architecture and was used as a men's residence hall. When the first Cary Hall opened in 1928, its 153 residents were greeted with multiple lounges, a billiards room, modern kitchen, trunk storage, and a special reception room for female guests. In addition to furniture, rooms came standard with a wastebasket, lamp, and globe. Room and board in this building came at a cost of $402 per year. 4 more buildings were built to complete the Cary Quadrangle. The entire quadrangle was r...
attributes.dedicationinfo: Frank and Jessie Levering Cary of Lafayette donated $50,000 to build the dormitory in memory of their son, Franklin Levering Cary. Franklin died suddenly of appendicitis shortly before his anticipated college enrollment date in 1912.

attributes.Name: Ophelia Duhme Residence Hall
attributes.description: Ophelia Duhme Residence hall is a four-story brick, stone, and reinforced concrete structure consisting of a central portion (42x32 ft.) and two wings each (42x109 ft.) with a fireproof roof. It contains 73 rooms, a main living room, two lounges with kitchenette, four reception rooms, a large recreation room, a completely equipped kitchen, a laundry room, and a four-bed infirmary. Originally designated as Women's Residence Hall South, the Women's Residence Halls were the first residence halls for women on Purdue's Campus. A lot of debate went in to planning this construction process and the fees associated with living in the new residence hall, as shown in the Board of Trustees Minutes. The building was renamed Ophelia Duhme Hall in 1942 and then Ophelia Duhme Residence Hall in 1969. All 5 women's residence halls were also referred to as Windsor Residence Halls on August 27,1969. Windsor was designed so that nearly every room in each hall would receive sunlight sometime during the d...
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building is dedicated to Ophelia Fowler Duhme who gifted land to the university in 1925. The funds acquired from this land were used to build a women's dormitory.

attributes.Name: Geoscience Annex
attributes.description: The Geoscience Annex was part of the FWA buildings that were brought to Purdue in 1947 as pre-engineered buildings which were leftover from World War II. They were remodeled by the physical facilities department to include lecture halls, classrooms and laboratories, and were intended to be temporary spaces to accommodate a growing student body. The buildings were erected with the help of student workers. Over the years, the buildings were used as chemistry and physics classrooms and laboratories, Naval Science and civil engineering spaces, the office for veterans administration, as warehouses, before becoming the home of the Creative Arts department. This building was also used as a pharmacy annex and geoscience annex during its existence. The Creative Arts buildings were demolished in 2004 by Dore and Associates of Bay City, Michigan for $289,600 in order to make space available for the construction of Neil Armstrong Hall of Engineering. The demolition was more expensive that acqui...

attributes.Name: Propulsion Research Laboratory
attributes.description: The Propulsion Research Laboratory was constructed to provide space for two rocket motor firing cells, a common control and instrument room, a small machine shop for rocket motor construction, a chemistry laboratory, and space for three onsite graduate student desks. Power was supplied to the building through a four-cylinder diesel electrical generator set that was obtained from the Navy. An army sound power field telephone was also used due to the lack of telephone service in the laboratory. An addition was made in 1951 to increase space for the machine shop, instrument storage, graduate student offices, two additional rocket motor cells, and control rooms. During this addition the building was also connected to the Universities power, water, and telephone services. The building was used for research on rockets, investigating high chamber pressure, heat transfer, and ignition characteristics of propellants and droplet combustion. This building is part of the Maurice J. Zucrow Labor...

attributes.Name: Richard Benbridge Wetherill Laboratory of Chemistry
attributes.description: A 3 part addition to the "New" Chemistry Building was completed in 1955 and the name was changed to Richard B. Wetherill Laboratory of Chemistry.The building was made of red brick, Indiana limestone, and red tiles that hide the laboratory vents on the roof. There are cut designs over the main doors that symbolize the 5 main branches of chemistry (a balance for analytical chemistry, a rat and leaf for biological chemistry, a portion of periodic table for inorganic chemistry, a tetrahedron for organic chemistry, and a phase diagram and thermodynamics equation for physical chemistry). There are also engraved names of 35 famous chemists going around 3 sides of the building (sides and front). Inside the front door, there are dark red Tennessee marble steps that bring students up to the main lecture hall which seats 463, and the entrance floor contains a bronze inlay depicting alchemists' symbols arranged in a circular pattern with crossed retorts. There are also four smaller lecture hall...

attributes.Name: Stewart Center
attributes.description: In 1958 a major addition was added to the University Library and the building became the Purdue Memorial Union - Hall of Music Annex. Construction began in 1954 and the new addition provided facilities for dramatic, musical, and forensic performances; exhibit and demonstration rooms; headquarters for the Division of Adult Education; student activities; and recreational and browsing rooms. The three floors in the central part of the building also provide new reading and study rooms. "The Spirit of the Land Grant College" mural was painted above the entrance to the HSSE library in the Stewart Center at a cost of $26,000. The mural was dedicated on October 4, 1961 and depicts the story of Purdue from the signing of the Morrill Act by Abraham Lincoln, to the education of its students, to the effects Purdue's education has upon the world. The mural was provided for by architect Walter Scholer and by treasurer R. B. Stewart, and was painted by Eugene Savage. The building was renamed the S...
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Stewart Center is named after R. B. Stewart who was a University Treasurer at Purdue University. Mr. and Mrs. Stewart also gifted their home, the Westwood Manor, and approximately thirty acres of wooded property to the university in 1971.

attributes.Name: Krannert Graduate School of Management
attributes.description: The Krannert Graduate School of management was built in 1965. It housed the School of Industrial Management at Purdue University. The School of Industrial Management was created in 1958 from the merger of the Department of Economics (established in the School of Science, Education, and Humanities in 1953) and the Department of Industrial Management and Transportation (part of the Schools of Engineering since 1956). The Krannert Graduate School of Industrial Administration was founded in 1962 with a $2.7 million endowment from Herman & Ellnora Krannert. The AACSB accredited the new school in 1967. In the early years, students were required to pursue a second major, in a technical subject, in addition to their coursework in business and management. The curriculum expanded over the following decade and the word "Industrial" was dropped from the schools' names in the mid 1970s. Today, the Krannert name refers to both the undergraduate and post-graduate programs. Krannert was reaccredite...
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building was named in honor of Mr. and Mrs. Herman C. Krannert whose gifts made its construction possible.

attributes.Name: Westwood Manor
attributes.description: The Westwood Manor was built in the 1932 and was the private home of Robert B. Stewart, the vice president for business and finance. In 1954, part of the land was deeded to the University and was used by the Department of Horticulture and Forestry and Conservation. Stewart later donated the home and grounds to the University after his retirement in 1971. At the time it was donated, it was was 6,959 square feet and valued at $1 million. The house was then remodeled and became the president's residence. In 1995 the Garden Room, a large hexagonal room with floor to ceiling windows, was added to the home. This room added an extra 10,000 square feet for entertaining guests. Since its donation to the university, four university presidents have lived at the Westwood manner. In 2007 the manor was renovated before President France A. Córdova and her husband, Chris Foster, moved in. The first level is dominated by spaces designed for large-scale entertaining, including two living rooms, a gar...

attributes.Name: Drew and Brittany Brees Student-Athlete Academic Center
attributes.description: The Drew and Brittany Brees Student-Athletic Academic Center was formerly called the Intercollegiate Athletic Facility and was built in 1980. This building contains the Holloway Gymnasium, named after Bob Holloway, a 1948 Purdue graduate. In 2012 the building was remodeled and the complex was renamed the Drew and Brittany Brees Student-Athletic Center. This remodel increased the academic study space from 3,150 square feet to 5,350 square feet. The Brees Center is located above Holloway Gymnasium and offers several academic support services for Purdue student-athletes. These supports include tutoring, mentoring, study areas/rooms, and advising offices. The computer lab in this building was dedicated in 2005 to honor Chris Ribnek, who served as academic support services director. In February 2018 the Purdue Board of Trustees approved a plan to renovate approximately 10,000 square feet on the first floor of the Center. The gift-funded $2.7 million project will create academic support s...
attributes.dedicationinfo: In 2012, the center was named the Drew and Brittany Brees Student-Athlete Academic Center in honor of Drew and Brittany's generous $2 million donation to support the continued academic success of 500-plus student-athletes.

attributes.Name: Ladies Hall
attributes.description: Ladies Hall was built in 1872 and contained a spacious dining room, a kitchen, laundry room, and other rooms expected to be associated with a boarding house. The hall also contained rooms for families, servants, members of the Faculty, and young ladies. However, only twenty ladies could be accommodated and all the women were supervised by a female member of the Purdue faculty. Ladies Hall also had a complete suite of rooms for the school of Industrial Art.
