This included a large lecture hall, four smaller rooms for shading and modeling in clay, an office, a library, and two basement rooms for special work.

attributes.Name: Ladies Hall
attributes.description: The northwest wing of Ladies hall was removed in 1922. Some records show that this wing was an addition and was removed because it was beyond repair. However, there is conflicting data on if this wing was an addition to the building and/or if it was torn down before the entire building was demolished in 1927. The main structure or the building was also repaired to meet the needs of the university until an adequate woman's building could be erected.

attributes.Name: Eliza Fowler Hall
attributes.description: Purdue Assembly Hall, renamed Fowler Hall, was completed in 1903. The purpose of the hall was to contain the administration offices of the University and rooms for the meetings of the faculty and trustees. The hall also expanded space for commencements, chapel services, and executive offices that were previously housed in University Hall. Fowler Hall also contained a pipe-organ and portrait of Mrs. Fowler. The building was demolished in 1954 to make room for the new Purdue Memorial Center which is now the Stewart Center. There is still an Eliza Fowler Hall within the Stewart Center building which sits approximately where the original structure was.
attributes.dedicationinfo: In 1901 Eliza Fowler, of Lafayette, donated money for the creation of a Purdue Assembly Hall (later renamed Fowler Hall). Fowler was a friend and business partner of John Purdue.

attributes.Name: Hall for Discovery and Learning Research
attributes.description: The Hall for Discovery and Learning Research is home to many projects and different groups. Some of these groups include AMI Purdue (Alfred Mann Institute for Biomedical Development), the Network for Earthquake Engineering Simulation, office space for the National Center for Nanotechnology, Healthcare Technical Assistance Program, the Center for Analytical Instrumentation Development, and Discovery Park/Office of the Vice President for Research staff.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building houses some of Purdue's top research projects which were announced at the dedication ceremony. France A. Cordova also spoke about how the building was built to adapt to the changing 21st century.

attributes.Name: Mechanical Engineering Building
attributes.description: The first Mechanical Engineering Building, also known as Heavilon Hall, opened in 1894. The building burned down on January 23, 1894, just four days after the dedication. The day after the fire, president James H. Smart said, "We are looking this morning to the future, not the past ... I tell you, young men, that tower shall go up one brick higher." Using money from donations and other forms of funding, the building was rebuilt for $148,102 and was nine bricks higher than the original.

attributes.Name: Horticultural Tool House
attributes.description: The Horticulture Tool House was located east of the Poultry Husbandry Building. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Dairy Barn
attributes.description: In 1905 the Dairy Barn was constructed. When it was built, it accommodated 20 animals and had concrete floors throughout. There were patent stalls and mangers, and a King system of ventilation. It contained good lighting, drainage systems, and facilities for the sanitary handling of milk.

attributes.Name: U.S Experiment Station
attributes.description: The U.S Experiment Station was the first Agricultural Experiment Station built on the West Lafayette Campus. It was a two-story brick structure with a glass vegetation house and green-houses. The station was equipped with laboratories and housed reports and technical documents for the School of Agriculture. The lower floor contained an office where meteorological instruments were kept, an agricultural museum, a seed room, and a tool room. The second floor contained a classroom, dissecting room, and room for the assistant in charge of the building and instruments. The rear portion of the building was a large 56 by 24 feet store room that was divided into small compartments for the storage of experimental plat products.

attributes.Name: Y.M.C.A. Building
attributes.description: This structure is the Y.M.C.A. Building that was on the corner of  State and Sheetz Street. No other information is currently available regarding this structure including exact start and end dates. This structure only appeared on Purdue's Map in a 1903 Y.M.C.A campus handbook.

attributes.Name: Heating and Power Plant-North
attributes.description: The North Heating and Power was added onto again in 1941. This addition added 2 new boilers and a new 2500 KW turbo generation to keep up with the growing need of the university. This came at a cost of a about $105,000 for the boilers and about $60,780 for the generator. The North Heating and Power Plant eventually became a secondary plant to the Heating and Power Plant-South (Walter W. Wade Utility Plant) and was only used for service. In 1970 the university started to abandon this power plant because the South Plant was becoming much more efficient. In 1991 the plant was taken fully out of operation for the first time but i was still used for monitoring purposes. In 1995 the Bell Tower was created as a new symbol of the Purdue campus in place of the iconic smokestack that accompanied Power Plant. The building was torn down in 2014 to make room for the Wilmeth Active Learning Center. Dr. James Mullins suggested incorporating the old smokestack from the North Heating and Power plant...

attributes.Name: Electrical Engineering
attributes.description: The first unit of the New Electrical Engineering building was completed in 1925. The first unit was comprised of a one story building with one general electric laboratory, one high voltage laboratory, and one lecture room with seats for four-hundred and eighty students. The second unit was completed in 1926.

attributes.Name: Men's Residence Hall Annex B
attributes.description: The Men's Residence Hall Annex B was acquired from Mr. and Mrs. Ralph B. Wiley in 1938 for $25,000. This building provided additional residence facilities for twenty men and an attached garage that was large enough for two cars. The house was operated in conjunction with the Franklin Levering Cary Quadrangle West Hall under the direction of the Men's Residence Halls. In 1946, this building became an infirmary. In 1948 the annexes could no longer be used for student housing because the placement of fire escapes was too expensive.

attributes.Name: Thomas S. and Harvey D. Wilmeth Active Learning Center
attributes.description: The Thomas S. and Harvey D. Wilmeth Active Learning Center is a multipurpose, adaptive library facility which is part of Purdue's IMPACT program. It is located at the heart of campus between Wetherill Hall of Chemistry and the Gatewood Wing of the Mechanical Engineering building. It is a student-centered space with 27 active learning classrooms, collaborative and study spaces, a Grand Reading Room with views of the clock tower, Au Bon Pain cafe and bakery with an open patio, the state of the art Maker Space and Geographical Information Visualization Center, and the Engineering and Science Library. The building is designed to have a highly efficient use of space, including a transition from classrooms to study spaces, and hosts a variety of activities, events, and versatile spaces for all Purdue University students.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building is dedicated to Thomas S. Wilmeth and Harvey D. Wilmeth who were brothers and Purdue graduates in the fields of Electrical and Chemical engineering respectively. The brothers founded Scot Industries, Inc. and were committed to expressing the importance of libraries and lifelong learning.

attributes.Name: Holleman-Niswonger Simulator Center
attributes.description: The Holleman-Niswonger Simulator Center is located at the Purdue Airport and serves students in the Professional Flight Program. It is a single-story building which contains thirteen total simulators, including three Cirrus SR20 simulators, one Phenom 100 simulator, and one CRJ-700 simulator. Each simulator has a nearby computer which records simulated flight, and a 12-foot-tall, hemispherical projection screen. All equipment in the simulators is accurate to 1/16 of an inch of the real planes' equipment.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building is dedicated to Scott M. Niswonger and Charles F. Holleman. Holleman was a faculty member in avaiaion and Niswonger was a Purdue graduate and CEO of the Landair Corporation.

attributes.Name: Waste Water Retention Tank
attributes.description: The Waste Water Retention Tank was built south of campus and sits next to the fuel oil tank and laboratory materials storage building. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Martin C. Jischke Hall of Biomedical Engineering
attributes.description: Martin C. Jischke Hall of Biomedical Engineering is a 92,000 square foot structure with four floors. It is located south of Herrick Laboratories and east of Intramural Drive.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Purdue University formally dedicated the home of its biomedical engineering program as the Martin C. Jischke Hall of Biomedical Engineering on Tuesday, September 30, 2008. The ceremony included the unveiling of a plaque and a portrait of the former Purdue president. The ceremony also marked the 10th anniversary of the biomedical engineering program at Purdue.

attributes.Name: Richard and Patricia Lawson Computer Science Building
attributes.description: The Richard and Patricia Lawson Computer Science Building was built to house the growing computer science department. This facility created a space for faculty and students to conduct research in the areas of bioinformatics, graphics, visualization, information security, software systems, and global computer networks. It also provided meeting rooms, four classrooms, five instructional labs, and four research labs.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building was dedicated to Richard and Patricia Lawson, who made a donation of $4.7 million to the building construction. Richard Lawson is a software industry executive who earned his Master's degree in computer science from Purdue in 1968.

attributes.Name: Franklin Levering Cary Quadrangle (West)
attributes.description: The Franklin Levering Cary Hall - West was the third building built in the Cary Quadrangle. This building has rooms for 155 students, all of which are furnished similarly to the first two buildings. When it was built, it also contained an office, a house manager's suite, a women's reception room, lounges, a dining room, and a fully equipped kitchen. Two more buildings were constructed to form the Cary Quadrangle in 1938 and 1939. The entire quadrangle was remodeled during a six year renovation project from 2000 to 2006.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Frank and Jessie Levering Cary of Lafayette donated $50,000 to build the dormitory in memory of their son, Franklin Levering Cary. Franklin died suddenly of appendicitis shortly before his anticipated college enrollment date in 1912.

attributes.Name: Amelia Earhart Residence Hall
attributes.description:
Amelia Earhart Residence Hall opened in 1964 and was named after the famous aviatrix Amelia Earhart. Amelia Earhart first came to Purdue University when the campus had an enrollment of 4,700 students and only one residence hall for women. In 1936, Amelia joined the Purdue staff and resided in what is now known as Duhme Hall in Windsor Residences. She began an association with the University in a dual role as consultant in careers for women and as technical adviser to the Department of Aeronautics.

Earhart Hall is one of University Residences that houses Learning Communities. Learning Communities are a great way to quickly become familiar with the Purdue campus and the multitude of activities available. A Learning Community is either a group of 20-30 first-year students who take two or three of the same courses together, a group of first-year students who share a common academic interest and live in the same residence hall, or a group of first-year students who take part in both of...
attributes.dedicationinfo:
Amelia Earhart taught many students. She seldom spoke of her achievements in aviation, but rather of vocational aptitudes, goals and careers for women. In 1936 the Purdue Research Foundation established the Amelia Earhart Fund for Aeronautical Research that made it possible for Amelia to purchase an Electra airplane, which she referred to as a "flying laboratory." It was equipped to do experimental work on speed and fuel consumption under varying conditions, television experimentation, the use of oxygen, radio communication and navigation instruments and methods, and the human equation of fatigue and endurance in relation to altitude, diet, sleep and eye strain.

A year later, when Amelia Earhart was on an around-the-world trip, the plane crashed on takeoff from Luke Field near Honolulu. Earhart and members of her crew were not injured. The plane was sent back to Los Angeles for repairs. Her second attempt at an around-the-world flight ended in her disappearance on July 2, 1937, whe...

attributes.Name: Spurgeon Golf Training Facility
attributes.description: The Tom Spurgeon Golf Training Center is located at the Birck Boilermaker Golf Complex. It includes team locker rooms, a lounge, a teaching room, coaches' offices, indoor putting greens, a heated driving bay, and exterior driving bays.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Tom Spurgeon is a Purdue alumnus who gave a lead gift of $750,000 toward the golf center. On May 21, 2004 ground was broken on the training center and a speech was made by Mr. Spurgeon himself.

attributes.Name: Frances M. Shealy Residence Hall
attributes.description: Frances M. Shealy Residence Hall was the second Women's Residence Hall, and was originally referred to as "North Hall" or "Women's Residence Halls Unit B". The Women's Residence Halls were the first residence halls for women on Purdue's Campus. A lot of debate went into planning this construction process and the fees associated with living in the new residence hall, as shown in the Board of Trustees Minutes. It was built in the English Tudor style and was constructed from brick and Indiana Limestone. A sculpture of a lion holding a shield in its paw sits above the front entrance. The building was renamed Frances M. Shealy Hall in 1949 and then Frances M. Shealy Residence Hall in 1969. All 5 women's residence halls were also referred to as Windsor Residence Halls on August 27,1969. Windsor was designed so that nearly every room in each hall would receive sunlight sometime during the day. A unique feature of four out of the five halls is that they line up in a straight line. If one we...
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building was named Frances M. Shealy Residence Hall in honor of the three Shealy sisters: Frances, Emma, and Josephine, daughters of Michael and Joanna Barry Shealy, of Delphi, Indiana. The sisters shared a mutual pledge that the last survivor would give her worldly possessions to a university in Indiana for the use of women students.

attributes.Name: Windsor Dining Court
attributes.description: The Vawter, Wood, and Warren Residence Halls were connected by a small structure in 1951.

attributes.Name: Melvin L. Ollman Golf Cart Barn
attributes.description: The Melvin L. Ollman Golf Cart Barn was built as part of the remodeling of the Kampen Golf Course. The cost of constructing the entire north course was $8.5 million and includes remodeling the golf course and building the Pete Dye club house, Melvin Ollman Golf Cart Barn, and the Samuel Voinoff Golf Pavilion.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The cart barn, also known as "Mel's Garage", was named after Melvin L. Ollman  who donated construction materials for the barn and clubhouse.

attributes.Name: Water Tower
attributes.description: The water tower, which was constructed in 1960, holds 1.5 million gallons of water. The water is used on campus for cooking, irrigation, washing and drinking. Originally, the tower was painted red and white in accordance with Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regulations. It was repainted white with a black and gold Motion P in 2001 after Purdue received permission from the FAA. The tower is repainted every 10 years.

attributes.Name: Jerry S. Rawls Hall
attributes.description: Rawls Hall is a four story structure that is home to all of the classes in the Krannert School of Management Master's program. It contains 13 electronically equipped classrooms, a professional career center, a multimedia based auditorium, 25 breakout rooms, distance learning facilities, and computer labs. The building was designed to to make the student learning experience a priority and to create a truly interactive environment.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Jerry S. Rawls graduated from the Purdue Krannert School of Management with a Master's degree and was the president and CEO of Finisar Corporation. He donated $10 million to the privately financed facility, and was a featured speaker at the dedication of the building.

attributes.Name: Yue-Kong Pao Hall of Visual and Performing Arts
attributes.description: Yue-Kong Pao Hall of Visual and Performing Arts was built in two phases. The building was opened after phase one was completed in 2003, and phase two began in 2004. Inside the building is a small practice theater, a music education classroom, a flexible studio theater, acting labs, supporting spaces, and a major 300-seat theater that replaced the facility in the basement of the Stewart Center. The building brings together art and design, dance, music, and theater and serves nearly 800 undergraduate majors.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building is dedicated to Yue-Kong Pao, a Chinese businessman and founder of the World-Wide Shipping Company. He is one of the 20th century's global leaders in the shipping industry and was respected for his honesty and skill in business. Mr. Pao also played an integral role in arranging President Ronald Reagan's visit to China in 1983. Mr. Pao had two daughters (Anna Pao Sohmen and Bessie Pao Woo) who graduated from Purdue in 1966 and 1971.

attributes.Name: Richard Owen Residence Hall
attributes.description: Originally called the Men's Residence Hall H-1, the Richard Owen Residence Hall is home to over 700 Purdue students. It is located on the north side of campus near the Slayter Center for the Performing Arts and Ford Dining Court.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Owen Residence Hall was named for Richard Owen, the first president of Purdue University. Mr. Owen was born in Scotland in 1810 and was the youngest of eight children. He immigrated to America and served in the U.S. Army during the Mexican War and the Civil War. He began working at Indiana University in 1864 and worked to establish the Agricultural and Normal school. The plans for this school became the first concept for Purdue University. He was also accomplished in the areas of geology, meteorology, and seismology.

attributes.Name: Burton D. Morgan Center for Entrepreneurship
attributes.description: The Burton D. Morgan Center for Entrepreneurship is a two-story, 31,000 square foot structure. It is located in Discovery Park and includes a 72 seat lecture room, a presentation room, faculty offices, and several conference and breakout rooms.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building is dedicated to Burton D. Morgan who graduated from Purdue University in 1938 with a degree in mechanical engineering. He was also awarded an honorary doctorate in management in 1992. He was an excellent entrepreneur who started 50 companies and wrote several books on entrepreneurship. Six of his companies have become major corporations, including Morgan Adhesives, which is one of the world's largest makers of pressure-sensitive adhesives. He also started the Burton D. Morgan Foundation, which awards grants to individuals in the areas of youth entrepreneurship, collegiate entrepreneurship, adult entrepreneurship, and the Hudson community.

attributes.Name: Fred and Mary Ford Dining Court
attributes.description: The Fred and Mary Ford Dining Court is a two-story building on the corner of Stadium Avenue and Russell Street. It contains seating for 800 people and is open to students, faculty, staff, and the community. The dining court is the first free-standing dining court on campus and offers a wide variety of food selections daily.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This buildings is named for Frederick R. and Mary Ford. Mr. Ford was the executive vice president and treasurer emeritus at Purdue University who earned a doctorate at Purdue's Krannert School of Management. Mrs. Ford graduated from Purdue in 1959 with a degree in Home Economics and was very involved with the School of Consumer and Family Sciences. Both Mr. and Mrs. Ford were active members of the Purdue community and made generous donations to the university.

attributes.Name: Pfendler Hall
attributes.description: Agricultural Hall was built in 1902. It was a two-story, 165-by-60 foot structure made of  brick and stone. It also had a front entrance and rear wing that were 30 x 40 feet. The building was heated and ventilated and originally contained offices for members of the Agricultural faculty, a library room, an auditorium seating 300, a large museum room, and halls for various agricultural societies. The building also housed classrooms and laboratories for instruction in agriculture, horticulture, live stock husbandry, veterinary hygiene, farm dairying, creamery work, and soil physics.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Agricultural Hall was renamed the David C. Pfendler Hall of Agriculture in 2001 and dedicated in 2004. Dean David C. Pfendler died in 1998 and worked in the School of Agriculture for 38 years before retiring as associate dean 1974.

attributes.Name: Roy L. Whistler Hall of Agricultural Research
attributes.description: The Roy L. Whistler Hall of Agricultural Research was built to increase the amount of space for research in agriculture. It is home to research in the fields of Agronomy, Biochemistry, Botany and Plant Pathology Entomology, and Horticulture and Agriculture. It contains 33 labs and laboratory complexes and encourages collaboration across disciplines and researchers.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building is dedicated to Dr. Roy L. Whistler. Dr. Whistler served many roles in the University including Faculty Representative to Intercollegiate Athletics. He was also given a number of awards in his field and was a distinguished member of the Purdue community.

attributes.Name: American Railway Building
attributes.description: Construction of the American Railway Building was completed in 1926 to house a new draft gear testing machine.

attributes.Name: Northwest Chiller Cooling Towers
attributes.description: The Northwest Chiller Cooling Towers were constructed south of Stadium Avenue and northwest of the France A. Córdova Recreational Sports Center.

attributes.Name: John W. Hicks Undergraduate Library
attributes.description: The John W. Hicks Undergraduate Library, originally called the Undergraduate Library, was built to serve undergraduate students at the university and store excess library materials. It was named the John W. Hicks Undergraduate Library in 1989.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building was named after John W. Hicks who served as the senior vice president of Purdue University until 1987. He held many other positions while at the university and graduated from Purdue with Master's and doctoral degrees in 1948 and 1950, respectively. Mr. Hicks also played and integral role in convincing the Indiana General Assembly to fund the undergraduate library.

attributes.Name: Clayton W. Dement Fire Station
attributes.description: The Clayton W. Dement Fire Station, originally the Fire Station Building, is a three-bay fire station.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Clayton W. Dement served as Purdue's first Superintendent of Safety and Security and later as Director of Buildings and Grounds, devoting a career spanning five decades to the enhancement of public safety and to the protection of University property. Clay personally guided the organization and development of the Purdue Police Department and the Purdue Fire Department, thereby providing the University community with the professional safety and security services both necessary and essential to its existence. More than any other person, Clay was responsible for the University's safety services and programs being recognized as among the finest of such services and programs offered by any institution of higher education.

attributes.Name: University Hall
attributes.description: Construction on University Hall began in the mid 1870s. Construction plans were halted in 1875 due to the Indiana legislature intervening in Purdue operations. The legislature was concerned with the disorganization of the university, poor record keeping, and high construction costs. Construction began again in 1876 once the building's plans were reviewed and, in 1877, the building was completed. The central portion of the building was five stories high with a basement and each end of the building was four stories high with an attic. The basement was made of stone and the other stories were made of brick with stone trimmings. The building also contained a chapel, assembly hall, galleries, academy hall, two society halls, a library, three cabinet rooms, eight recitation rooms, two well lit basement rooms, and two suites with lunch and toilet rooms. In 1923, the building was completely redecorated, the heating system was improved, and gas lights were replaced with electrical lights in...

attributes.Name: Leo Philip Doyle Laboratory
attributes.description: This building was originally called the Veterinary Food Storage Building, the Leo Phillip Doyle Laboratory was built as part of a large construction project to create multiple buildings to be used for the school of Veterinary Science and Medicine. The total cost of constructing the Veterinary Medicine buildings was $5,485,000. It was renamed the Leo Philip Doyle Laboratory in 1988 because the previous name no longer related to the use of its offices and research laboratories.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building was named after Leo Philip Doyle who was a well renowned scientist at Purdue.

attributes.Name: Helen R. Johnson Hall of Nursing
attributes.description: Originally called the Nursing and Allied Health Sciences Building, the Helen R. Johnson Hall of Nursing was constructed to house the Department of Nursing in the School of Technology. When it was built it contained conference rooms, classrooms, offices, and work spaces. It was renamed the Helen R. Johnson Hall of Nursing in 1990.
attributes.dedicationinfo: In 1990 the Nursing and Allied Health Sciences Building was renamed the Helen R. Johnson Hall of Nursing. Dr. Johnson was employed by Purdue University in 1962 to implement an Associate's degree program in nursing. She also served as the head of the department until 1979 and retired in 1980.

attributes.Name: Veterinary Pathology Building
attributes.description: Previously known as the Veterinary Building and then as the Veterinary Sciences Building, the Veterinary Pathology Building is located on Harrison Street. The building was two stories with a basement and attic that was used for dissecting. When it was built, the building contained class rooms, laboratories, offices, a clinic and box stalls for animals. The building supplied much needed facilities for instruction in anatomy, physiology, veterinary science and medicine.

attributes.Name: Biochemistry Building
attributes.description: The Biochemistry Building, that was formerly named the Agricultural Chemistry Building, was expanded in 1981. The building was expanded by 18,000 square feet and included the completion of the third floor.

attributes.Name: Purdue Village Administration Building
attributes.description: The Purdue Village Administration Building provided 23,000 gross square feet of new space for the Married Student Housing. The building housed the Married Student Housing administrative offices, storage areas for furniture, plumbing fixtures, electrical supplies, appliances, paint, plaster, and cleaning equipment; and storage/service area for grounds maintenance. The facility also provided storage space for the Residence Halls.

attributes.Name: Herbert C. Brown Laboratory of Chemistry
attributes.description: Originally called the Chemistry Building 2 and Chemistry Building East, the Herbert C. Brown Laboratory of Chemistry was built directly east of the Richard Benbridge Wetherill Lab of Chemistry. It was named Herbert C. Brown Laboratory of Chemistry in 1986.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building was dedicated to Dr. Herbert C. Brown, a Purdue professor that won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work in hydroboration chemistry.

attributes.Name: Terminal Building
attributes.description: The Terminal Building was built as a new hangar and operations building that met the needs of the Purdue Airport. The building provided reading rooms, mess halls, offices, hangar space, and barracks. This accommodated additional classrooms, shops, Link Laboratories, and aircraft storage.

attributes.Name: Beering Hall
attributes.description: Originally called the Classroom/Office Building, Beering Hall was built in 1993. It houses offices, classrooms, computing labs, and the Deans' offices for Purdue's College of Liberal Arts and College of Education. It was renamed the Liberal Arts and Education Building in 1992 and Steven C. Beering Hall of Liberal Arts and Education in 2002.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Purdue University Board of Trustees dedicated a classroom-office building on the West Lafayette campus in honor of Purdue President Emeritus Steven C. Beering. He served Purdue for more than 17 years, during which more than 20 buildings were added to the campus, including the Liberal Arts and Education Building that bears his name. Thirteen more facilities were either expanded or renovated. During that same period, enrollment in liberal arts grew to make it one of the largest schools on campus and the School of Education was created.

attributes.Name: University Street Parking Garage
attributes.description: The University Parking Garage was constructed on Waldron Street and Third Street in 1969. This parking garage needed to be constructed earlier than expected due to an unexpected increase in enrollment in 1967 and an anticipated increase in 1968. This garage had parking spaces for 503 cars.

attributes.Name: Ward L. Lambert Field House & Gymnasium
attributes.description: Originally called the Fieldhouse and Gymnasium for Men, this structure was made of stone, brick, steel, and reinforced concrete. When it was built, it consisted of a one-story fieldhouse and a 110 by 210 foot, four-story gymnasium section. It also contained the offices of the Division of Physical Education for Men, training areas, locker and shower rooms, classrooms, several small gymnasiums, a large gymnasium, an Olympic-size swimming pool with complete water conditioning equipment, and a 172 by 303 foot fieldhouse with an unobstructed floor which will seat 8,500 people for basketball games. It was erected as a Public Work Administration (PWA) project and was remodeled in 1999 to improve its timing system. On February 24, 1947 the east wooden bleachers collapsed during the halftime of a basketball game against the University of Wisconsin-Madison. Three people were killed and over 250 others were injured.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building was named after Ward L. Lambert who was a legendary former Purdue basketball coach.

attributes.Name: Forest Products Building
attributes.description: When the Forest Products Building was built, it was a two-story brick building. On the first floor, there were two large laboratories, one of which is devoted to heavy farm machinery, and the other to work with cement. On the second floor, there was a light farm machinery laboratory, a large well-lit drawing room and two classrooms. In the building there are also offices, small laboratories, and locker and tool rooms. It currently contains the Wood Research Laboratory which researches the product and process engineering of wood products and the historic restoration and preservation of wood.

attributes.Name: Morgan J. Burke Aquatic Center
attributes.description: The Boilermaker Aquatic Center was built in 2001 and significantly improved Purdue's swimming and diving facilities. The Aquatic Center serves as a home to the men and women's swimming and diving programs and all recreational and educational swimming.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Boilermaker Aquatic Center and the Doris Z. Holloway Pool were dedicated in ceremonies attended by more than 1,000 people in 2001. On May 5, 2017 the facility was renamed the Morgan J. Burke Aquatic Center in honor of Morgan Burke. Burke was a Purdue swimmer, swim team captain, vice president, and athletics director.

attributes.Name: Purdue West Building F
attributes.description: The Purdue West Building F was the third Purdue West building that was built on the west side of campus near John T. McCutcheon Residence Hall. It is now home to Subway and Fishya.

attributes.Name: Walter W. Wade Utility Plant
attributes.description: An addition to the Walter W. Wade Utility Plant was completed in 1977.
attributes.dedicationinfo: "Walter W. Wade served as Purdue's first Vice President of Physical Facilities, guiding the University through three and one-half decades of uninterrupted construction and campus development. Through his actions and personal effort, Walt established the highest standards for the maintenance, operation and construction of Purdue facilities. These high standards for plant engineering and management are recognized nationally and have saved the University millions of dollars, thereby earning for Purdue the great respect and sincere appreciation of the taxpayers of the state of Indiana."

attributes.Name: Martha E. and Eugene K. Warren Residence Hall
attributes.description: Originally designated as Women's Residence Hall D, Warren Hall was built with Vawter Hall to accommodate more women students. This building was officially named Martha E. and Eugene K. Warren Residence Hall in November 1954 after Mr. Warren died. The Women's Residence Halls were the first residence halls for women on Purdue's Campus. Much debate went in to planning this construction process and the fees associated with living in the new residence hall, as shown in the Board of Trustees Minutes. All 5 women's residence halls were referred to as Windsor Residence Halls on August 27,1969. The Windsor complex was designed so that nearly every room in each hall would receive sunlight at some time during the day. Four of the Five halls in the Windsor complex line up in a straight line. If one were to open the lobby doors in Duhme, Shealy, Warren, and Vawter, you would be able to "shoot an arrow in a straight line through all of them."
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building is named after Martha E. and Eugene K. Warren. Mr. and Mrs. Warren gave their stock in the West Lafayette Water Works to the University as a generous gift. This donation was used to partially fund the Warren Residence Hall.

attributes.Name: Early Care and Education Center
attributes.description: The Early Care and Education Center is located north of State Street at the corner of State Street and Dexter Lane. The planning, design and construction of the new child care facility was requested by the Board of Committee and Trustees in February 2015. The exact date of construction is unknown and no other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Westwood Manor Garage
attributes.description: The Westwood Manor Garage was built with the Westwood Manor. The Westwood Manor was the private home of Robert B. Stewart, the vice president for business and finance. In 1971, after his retirement, Stewart donated the home and grounds to the University.

attributes.Name: Edward C. Elliott Hall Of Music
attributes.description: The Edward C. Elliott Hall Of Music, originally the Hall of Music, is a five-story, 280-by-190-foot structure with an air-conditioned main auditorium, balcony, and gallery. When it was built it contained seating for 6,148 people, band instruments, practice rooms, main radio broadcasting studios, offices, dressing rooms, and band drill rooms. It was erected as a Public Works Administration (PWA) project and was renamed the Elliott Hall of Music in 1958.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The dedication of the Hall of Music took place over two nights, May 3 and 4, of 1940. The dedication consisted of two concerts, one on each night. On the night of Friday, May 3, the Purdue Military Band and Purdue Choir opened the dedication ceremony, followed by performances by Lawrence Tibbett and Helen Jepson. On the evening of Saturday, May 4, a representative of the Public Works Association, Indiana State Governor, and President of the Board of Trustees presided over the dedication ceremony. The concert that followed was performed by Nino Martini and Helen Jepson. The building was renamed the Elliott Hall of Music in 1958 after Edward C. Elliott. Mr. Elliott was the President of the University from 1922 to 1945 and played an integral role in planning and obtaining funds for the Hall of Music.

attributes.Name: Frederick L. Hovde Hall of Administration
attributes.description: Originally called the Student Services and Administration Building, the Frederick L. Hovde Hall of Administration is a 70 by 230 foot, four-story building that was erected as part of a PWA project. It contains a Board of Trustees' room and offices for the Dean of Men, the Dean of Women, the Office of the President of the University, the Controller, the Purchasing Department, the Accounting Department, Personnel for Men, Personnel for Women, and the Student Health Service. The basement is used for the filing and storage of records. It was designated as the Executive Building in 1936 and renamed the Hovde Hall of Administration on April 26, 1975.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Room 102 is named the Howard Lyon Conference room after Howard Lyon, who was the vice president for business services and assistant treasurer from 1985-1993. He was also the vice president for management information and long-range budget planning from 1993 until his death in June 1995. The building was renamed the Frederick L. Hovde Hall of Administration in 1975 after Frederick Hovde who was the President at Purdue University from 1946-1971.

attributes.Name: First Street Towers Central
attributes.description: This structure is part of the First Street Towers complex and was designed with upperclassmen in mind. These towers have single air-conditioned rooms with private baths are arranged in clusters of no more than 22 students around a central living room/dinette area. The total cost of constructing the East and Central towers was $52,000,000.

attributes.Name: Purdue West Building C
attributes.description: The Purdue West Building C shopping center was the fifth Purdue West building that was built on the west side of campus near John T. McCutcheon Residence Hall. It is now home to GNC.

attributes.Name: Purdue Shopping Center
attributes.description: The first Purdue West building was built on the west side of campus near John T. McCutcheon Residence Hall in 1958.

attributes.Name: Purdue Shopping Center
attributes.description: The second Purdue West building was built on the west side of campus near John T. McCutcheon Residence Hall in 1959.

attributes.Name: Purdue West Building D
attributes.description: The Purdue West Building D shopping center was the fourth Purdue West building that was built on the west side of campus near John T. McCutcheon Residence Hall. It is now home to Purdue Parking Facilities, University Spirit, and Papa John's Pizza.

attributes.Name: France A. Córdova Recreational Sports Center
attributes.description: A multi-phase addition and renovation to the Recreational Gymnasium was completed in 2012. The addition was needed to move Purdue's recreational facilities closer to other Big Ten schools' standards. This addition included enhancing cardiovascular fitness space, free weight, indoor jogging/walking, group exercise/multipurpose space, and basketball courts. There was also upgrades to the racquetball courts, gym space and venues, and additional spaces for locker rooms, wellness space, free zone/common space, and food and dining areas. Besides adding space and equipment, the expansion added new concepts to the gymnasium. These new concepts included connecting the east and west entrances with an atrium that is open to everyone and offers healthy snacks and accessible health and wellness services. During the renovation, it was renamed the France A. Córdova Recreational Sports Center. It is affectionately known on campus as the Co-Rec.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building is named after past Purdue President France A. Córdova. Córdova served as the University President from July 2007 to July 2012. She encouraged students to pursue their interest in the Recreation Sports Center project and helped to convince the state and Purdue trustees of the need for the renovation.

attributes.Name: Hazardous Material Management Trailer
attributes.description: The Hazardous Materials Management Trailer is located north of the Laboratory Materials Storage Building and northeast of the Waste Water Retention Tank. Inside of the trailer, all hazardous waste is processed and disposed of in an environmentally friendly way.

attributes.Name: Locomotive Testing Plant
attributes.description: The Locomotive Testing Plant was built in 1895 and was the second testing plant for locomotives. The original locomotive testing plant was located in Heavilon Hall which burned down just a few days after its dedication. The new plant contained equipment to house large locomotives and study their performance. The performance could be tested while the engine was running at any desired speed and under any load. This testing plant contained 36 steam cylinders, six friction brakes, and six surface condensers. At the time the original building was built in 1891, there were no tracks that lead into campus. Because of this, Schenectady No. 1 was lifted off of the tracks and placed on skids to be dragged about a mile and a half across country. A school holiday was declared so every able-bodied student could assist in the transfer. During World War II, highly secret research on the atomic bomb occurred in the testing plant that was referred to as "The Castle." The roof of this building had re...

attributes.Name: John Purdue Grave
attributes.description: The grave of university benefactor John Purdue is located south of University Hall on Memorial Mall. John Purdue, the namesake of the university, lived from 1802 to 1876. A fountain, seating area, and statue of Purdue himself are nearby. The statue was made possible by alumni, friends, and the Order of the Iron Key Class of 2012 members.

attributes.Name: Science Annex
attributes.description: The Science Annex was a brick building located east if the pharmacy building that was built in 1873. It had 2 floors and provided recitation rooms, department offices, and laboratories for sewing and work in nutrition for the students in Home Economics.

attributes.Name: Grounds Maintenance
attributes.description: The Grounds Maintenance Facility was built in order to relocate the Grounds Department and Printing Services. This created extra space for instructional buildings on campus.

attributes.Name: Heating Plant
attributes.description: The Heating and Power Plant was built in 1962 to increase the Power Plant capacity of the University and to keep up with the progress of  construction.

attributes.Name: Mechanical Lab
attributes.description: Mechanic's Hall was built in 1886. The building contained recitation rooms, drawing rooms, shop rooms, a testing laboratory, and an office. All the rooms were built using high walls, good lighting, and good ventilation. The drawing rooms (24 x 33 feet) were furnished with tables, drawing boards and T-squares for each student. There was also a supply of the more expensive drawing instruments such as odontographs, proportional dividers, protractors, beam compasses, rubber curves, etc. In the building there was a wood-working room, a foundry, a forge-room, a machine room, an engine-room, a tool room, and a coat room. The wood working room contained twenty benches, with full sets of bench tools for wood, eleven lathes for turning, a grindstone, a circular saw, and a scroll saw. The foundry was equipped with a cupola furnace for iron, a crucible furnace for brass, a core oven, and a full supply of sand, flasks and molder's tools. The forge room contained fourteen forges with power suppli...

attributes.Name: Transportation Maintenance Building
attributes.description: This building provides lubricating facilities, wash racks, truck and car tire repair, tool storage, bulk and parts storage, a safety check lane, grease racks, office and employee area and general mechanic-preventive maintenance work space.

attributes.Name: Electrical Laboratory
attributes.description: The original portion of the first electrical engineering building was completed in 1890. When it was built it was used for studies in the school of Electrical Engineering, and consisted of a dynamo room, drawing, and recitation rooms.

attributes.Name: Electrical Engineering
attributes.description: A large addition was added to the Electrical Laboratory in 1906. It was a three-story stone and brick building attached to a one story brick structure, with a basement. It contained instrument rooms, a calibration room, laboratories, a seminary room, offices, rooms for electrical design, and lecture and recitation rooms. The one-story wing contained a large lecture hall which seated 300 students. The building was remodeled in 1926 for classroom use at the President's discretion. In 1950 the building was torn down to make room for the 3 part addition to the "New" Chemistry building.

attributes.Name: State Street Office Facility
attributes.description: The State Street Office Facility was built along State Street across from the Horticulture Park and near Dexter Lane. It was torn down in January 2020 to make way for the Provenance development. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Nuclear Engineering Building
attributes.description: The Nuclear Engineering Building was originally named the Engineering Science Shop Building #1. It went through several name changes such as the Engineering Sciences Building, Aeronautical and Engineering Sciences Building, and finally the Nuclear Engineering Building.

attributes.Name: Michael Golden Engineering Laboratories and Shops
attributes.description: In 1982 the eastern part of the building, Michael Golden Hall, was torn down. The western end, the Michael Golden Engineering Laboratories and Shops, remained and 2,600 feet of the south wing were remodeled to create a robotics lab.

attributes.Name: Agricultural and Biological Engineering Building
attributes.description: A large addition was added to the Agricultural Engineering building in 1941. The building was renamed the Agricultural and Biological Engineering building in 1996 after the department was renamed the previous spring. In 2018 the one story part of the building was torn down to make room for a multi-level addition.

attributes.Name: Drug Discovery Building
attributes.description: The Drug Discovery building is a three-story building that houses biomedical engineering, medicinal chemistry, and fluorescence-guided surgery. The building has over 100 staff members and is one of the first of its kind at a university. It also contains a wide range of research on various diseases.

attributes.Name: Grounds Maintenance Greenhouse Facility
attributes.description: The Grounds Maintenance Greenhouse Facility is located west of  the Grounds Maintenance Facility. No other information is currently available regarding this building.

attributes.Name: Stuart Field
attributes.description: Stuart Field, also known as the Grand Stand, was the center for recreation in the early 20th century. The field hosted baseball and football games, was the practice field for the Purdue Student Artillery Training Corps and ROTC. It was also a focal point for student activities until its demolition in 1924 following the completion of Ross-Ade Stadium. The field was improved in 1895 and a grand stand was added to the field in 1898.

attributes.Name: Peirce Hall
attributes.description: A small addition was added to the Stanley Coulter Annex in 1980. At this time the building was renamed Peirce Hall.

attributes.Name: Peirce Hall
attributes.description: The southern portion of Peirce Hall (the original Physics Building) was removed. The Class of 1950 Lecture Hall was built in its place.

attributes.Name: Stanley Coulter Annex
attributes.description: An addition was added to the north end of the Physics Building in 1935. This addition later became part of Peirce Hall.

attributes.Name: Dick and Sandy Dauch Alumni Center
attributes.description: The Dick and Sandy Dauch Alumni Center is a three-story building constructed out of brick with glass accents. The center is home to the Purdue Alumni Association and is the first alumni center at the university. The Spurgeon Hall of Spirit is located within and showcases Purdue traditions, athletics, and history of the University. There are five exhibits/alcoves on display to pay tribute various aspects of Purdue. The exhibits include: one dedicated to Purdue astronauts, an exhibit called "Beginners" with the history of Purdue, a "Traditions" alcove featuring Purdue traditions, an "Athletics Alcove" highlighting the Purdue Athletic program, and a "Discovery Alcove" that highlights the science and research at the university.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building is dedicated to Dick and Sandy Dauch, the lead donors for the Alumni Center. As stated in the Board of Trustees meeting minutes, "the Dauches personify all that (the Alumni Center) promises to celebrate: great achievement on campus and beyond, school pride and loyalty - past, present, and future - and ongoing community service in the broadest sense." Dick graduated from Purdue in 1964 with a degree in industrial management. He also led a successful career in the automotive industry.

attributes.Name: Everett B. Vawter Residence Hall
attributes.description: Originally called Residence Hall E, the Everett B. Vawter Residence Hall was constructed alongside Residence Hall D. This residence hall is part of the Windsor Residence Halls that were the first residence halls for women on Purdue's Campus. A lot of debate went in to planning this construction process and the fees associated with living in the new residence hall, as shown in the Board of Trustees Minutes. All 5 women's residence halls were also referred to as Windsor Residence Halls on August 27,1969. The Windsor complex was designed so that nearly every room in each hall would receive sunlight sometime during the day. Four of the Five halls in the Windsor complex line up in a straight line. If one were to open the lobby doors in Duhme, Shealy, Warren, and Vawter, you would be able to "shoot an arrow in a straight line through all of them."
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Vawter Residence Hall was named after Wallace Vawter's father, Everett B. Vawter, who was a lifetime resident of West Lafayette. Wallace R. Vawter and Helen Cripe Vawter made a gift to the Purdue Research Foundation of 1,693 shares of West Lafayette Water Company, Inc., stock that was valued at $190,000.

attributes.Name: Arthur G. Hansen Life Sciences Research Building
attributes.description: The Arthur G. Hansen Life Sciences Research Building houses the Purdue University Center for Cancer Research, a National Cancer Institute designated cancer center. The building is four-stories tall and contains multidisciplinary laboratory spaces. The building also houses the Transgenic Mouse Core Facility, the Bioscience Imaging Facility, an Nuclear Magnetic Resonance facility, and an animal facility; all of which support the drug discovery efforts at Purdue.
attributes.dedicationinfo: In 2002 Arthur G. Hansen honored Purdue and his wife, Nancy, by donating $1.8 million to build the proscenium theater in Yue-Kong Pao Hall, which now bears his wife's name.

attributes.Name: Aspire at Discovery Park A
attributes.description: Aspire at Discovery Park is 387,000 sq. ft. apartment community on the Purdue campus to feature tech-centric living with an integrated smart home experience for students and residents to meet the growing demand for technology-driven, connected living spaces in the higher education arena.

attributes.Name: University Church
attributes.description: University Church was founded in 1919, part of the Presbyterian Church’s Westminster Foundation campus ministry. University Church broke ground on its first building on the property in 1939. The sanctuary was built in 1959. The property of University Church was purchased May 1, 2014 by Purdue for $2.4 million. It was home to the Campus Christian Fellowship (CCF) an open group of young adults committed to and serving the interdenominational ministry. The building was then used by The Anvil, a student-led entrepreneurial organization, before being used by the university for instructional space beginning in 2021.

attributes.Name: Convergence Center for Innovation and Collaboration
attributes.description: The Convergence Center for Innovation and Collaboration is a 5-story building at 101 Foundry Drive that serves as the entryway to the university for those interested in technology commercialization and startups. The center is a resource hub for innovation, technology commercialization and entrepreneurial activities, and includes a large lobby and plaza spaces for engagement and business activity and retail space on the first floor.

attributes.Name: Purdue Village Community Center
attributes.description: The Purdue Village Community Center held activities of the Purdue Village Apartment Complex. This space was available for residents for studying and small group meetings and also had a fitness room, recreation room, and a gathering space for residents.

attributes.Name: Winifred Parker Residence Hall
attributes.description: Originally under the project named Vawter Field Housing, the Winifred Parker Residence Hall was built in 2015. It is a residence hall that was built to focus on student learning and academic success. When it was built the residence hall contained 304 beds, learning communities, a Starbucks coffee shop, and the Third Street Market which was relocated from Meredith Hall. The rooms contain space for four students and were designed in a semi-suite and suite style. Each semi-suite contains two bedrooms and a shared bathroom and suites also contain a shared living room.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building was re-dedicated in October 2021 as Winifred Parker Residence Hall in honor of Purdue graduate Winifred Parker. Parker, along with her sister Freida, successfully worked to integrate Purdue University residence halls in 1947.

attributes.Name: Kozuch Football Performance Complex
attributes.description: The Football Performance Complex is a three level building adjoined to the north end of Mollenkopf Athletic Center. It includes a locker room, weight room, coaching offices, meeting rooms, a player development room, equipment areas, and a space for sports medicine. The building's purpose is to centralize all football activities. The Football Performance Complex was designed by the Populous architectural firm who alos designed the Aviva Stadium in Dublin, the Jacksonville Jaguars Amphitheater and Flex Field, Yankee Stadium, and the London and Sochi Olympic Stadiums.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The Purdue Board of Trustees approved the naming the Football Performance Complex the Kozuch Football Performance Complex in recognition of an anonymous, very generous gift from a donor.

attributes.Name: Ernest C. Young Hall
attributes.description: Originally called Graduate House, the Ernest C. Young Hall is 10 stories high. When it was built, it contained offices, classrooms, lounge areas, meeting rooms, and dormitory space for approximately 700 graduate students. In 2003 floors six, seven and eight were renovated, in 2007 floors nine and 10 were renovated, and in 2012 a $4.5 million project began to renovate the second and third floors.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building is named after Ernest C. Young, who was the Dean of Purdue's graduate school from 1942 until he retired, and the first Vice President for Research at the University in 1961. Mr. Young was accomplished in the fields of agricultural economics and farm management and helped to guide the structure of Purdue's graduate education.

attributes.Name: Electrical Engineering
attributes.description: An addition to the Electrical Engineering Building was built in 1931. This particular addition added the Thomas Duncan Laboratory of Electrical Measurements. The laboratory was a three-story brick, stone, and reinforced concrete structure that was 18,600 square feet. It contains a fireproof roof, a lecture room, museum room, offices laboratories, classrooms, and small research laboratories. It later became a reading and study room and displayed Duncan's inventions.

attributes.Name: Electrical Engineering
attributes.description: Two sections were added to the south wing of the building in 1942. The addition was made of reinforced concrete floors and brick walls. The second section was a High-Voltage Laboratory that was joined to the main building with a one-story connection. This section was made of a structural steel frame with non-bearing face brick and concrete walls. It is 121 x 61 ft. and 60 ft. high from the basement to the top of roof. In 1986 a bridge was added to connect this building to the Materials and Electrical Engineering building.

attributes.Name: Max W and Maileen Brown Family Hall
attributes.description: A loading dock  was added to the southwest side of the Electrical Engineering building. No other information is currently available regarding this structure.

attributes.Name: Purdue Village Preschool
attributes.description: The Purdue Village Preschool was originally designed to be a nursery for residents of Married Student Courts. The building has gone through multiple functions and name changes and is currently a preschool for the children of Purdue Village residents, Purdue students, Purdue faculty, and the general public.

attributes.Name: Patty Jischke Early Care and Education Center
attributes.description: The Patty Jischke Early Care and Education Center contained seven classrooms for infants, toddlers, and preschoolers. The various rooms had a capacity of eight to twenty children. Following the creation of a new Jischke Early Care and Education Center northwest of campus in August 2022 this building was decommissioned.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The childcare center was named in honor of former First Lady of Purdue, Patty Jischke.

attributes.Name: Helen B. Schleman Hall
attributes.description: Helen B. Schleman Hall, formerly the Recitation Building, is a three-story, dark brick and stone building, with terracotta ornamentation, a tile roof and reinforced concrete construction inside. When it was built, it contained 26 classrooms and 8 offices and was located north of University Hall. The building originally housed the departments of Education, History, Economics, and Mathematics. The building name changed on December 19, 2022 to Schleman Hall as the Dean of Students Office moved from its prior location in the previous Helen B. Schleman Hall of Student Services.

attributes.Name: Data Science
attributes.description: A large addition was added to the building that was formerly known as the Pharmacy, Student Services, and Geosciences Building. When the addition was added the building was renamed the Helen B. Schleman Hall of Student Services. In December 2022 all students services offices were relocated across campus, and the building was renamed Data Science. The Recitation Building was renamed Helen B. Schleman Hall.
attributes.dedicationinfo: The building was dedicated to Helen B. Schleman, Dean Emerita of Women.  "After completing her deanship, Helen Schleman remained at Purdue, working half-time for two years as director of Span Plan, a program she conceived and launched. She designed this program to assist mature women who had left or who had never entered college to enroll with the goal of completing one or more degrees. She encouraged them to think in different terms about themselves and their potential. Through her efforts, funds were raised to provide financial assistance for those who needed it, as well as academic and personal counseling. Her dedication to Span Plan assured its success, and it continues to provide special attention to both mature women and men as they enter or return to college seeking to make lives more productive."

attributes.Name: Ground Service Building
attributes.description: Two large storage sheds were removed from the grounds service building in 2012. No other information is currently available regarding the removal of these sheds.

attributes.Name: Heavilon Hall
attributes.description: The third building referred to as Heavilon Hall on Purdue's Campus was erected in 1959. The first building burned down four days after it was dedicated and the second Heavilon Hall was partially torn down in 1956 to make room for this building and as then fully torn down in 1969. This building originally housed the Departments of English and Speech, and the Speech and Hearing Clinic. Other related activities such as debating, developmental reading, and research in speech and hearing disorders were also conducted in this building.
attributes.dedicationinfo: Heavilon Hall is named after Amos Heavilon who gave $35,000 to Purdue University in 1892. This money was applied to the construction costs of the Old Mechanical Engineering building, also known as Heavilon Hall.

attributes.Name: Grounds Service Building
attributes.description: The Grounds Service Building was built in 1910. When it was built, it was a brick building with a tile roof and steam heat located at the center of the building.The ground floor contained an office and sleeping rooms for the Superintendent of Livestock, wash and locker rooms for students, a boiler room, and a large judging arena with a tan bark floor. It was 120 x 40 feet and had 1,000 seats arranged in an amphitheater style. The space under the seats on the south and west ends contained box stalls with outside doors. The north and east end contained preparation and demonstration rooms. The second floor of the front part of the building contains a large classroom.

attributes.Name: Birck Nanotechnology Center
attributes.description: The Birck Nanotechnology Center is located in Discovery Park and is a two-story facility. It is used for interdisciplinary research and contains cleanrooms, chemistry and biology laboratories, epitaxy laboratories, metrology laboratories, instructional laboratories, and incubator laboratories.

attributes.Name: Krannert Center for Executive Education and Research
attributes.description: The Krannert Center for Executive Education and Research was built to house executive education programs. It contained two large arena-style classrooms and small meeting rooms for group discussion, along with interactive computer facilities in every room. The main lounge in the building was used for informal gatherings, receptions, guest speakers, and formal banquets.
attributes.dedicationinfo: This building is named for Herman C. Krannert who founded the Krannert Charitable Trust. Donations from the Krannert Charitable Trust were used to completely finance the building.
